title: MapTCL: Temporal Consistency Learning via Bidirectional Alignment for Vectorized HD Map Construction
comment: Accepted at 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: Constructing reliable online HD maps remains challenging in dynamic urban environments due to moving objects and occlusions. While recent works employ feature-level temporal fusion to address this, they rely solely on per-frame ground truth supervision. Consequently, they lack an explicit objective to directly penalize the geometric noise and temporal jitter between consecutive online HD maps. To address this, we propose MapTCL, an auxiliary training strategy that formulates temporal consistency loss between current and past frames via bidirectional alignment. Specifically, Bidirectional Vector Consistency Learning (BVCL) models the geometric and semantic discrepancies between associated past and current vector instances as an auxiliary loss. We also employ Raster map Consistency Learning (RCL) as an additional loss to stabilize dense BEV features. By jointly training with these dual losses, MapTCL improves the temporal stability of generated HD maps. Extensive experiments on two standard benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. As a versatile plug-and-play module, MapTCL consistently enhances existing baseline models, achieving gains of +3.7 mAP & +2.8 C-mAP on nuScenes and +3.1 mAP & +2.5 C-mAP on Argoverse 2 without additional inference overhead.

AI.tldr: MapTCL is an auxiliary training strategy that improves temporal consistency of online HD map construction by introducing dual losses—Bidirectional Vector Consistency Learning (BVCL) and Raster map Consistency Learning (RCL)—to directly penalize geometric noise and temporal jitter between consecutive frames.
AI.motivation: Existing feature-level temporal fusion methods for online HD mapping rely solely on per-frame ground truth supervision, lacking an explicit objective to penalize geometric noise and temporal jitter between consecutive online HD maps in dynamic urban environments.
AI.method: MapTCL formulates a temporal consistency loss between current and past frames via bidirectional alignment. It uses (1) Bidirectional Vector Consistency Learning (BVCL) to model geometric and semantic discrepancies between associated past and current vector instances, and (2) Raster map Consistency Learning (RCL) to stabilize dense BEV features. These dual losses are applied as auxiliary training objectives.
AI.result: MapTCL achieves significant gains on two standard benchmarks: +3.7 mAP & +2.8 C-mAP on nuScenes and +3.1 mAP & +2.5 C-mAP on Argoverse 2, consistently improving various baseline models without additional inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: MapTCL is a versatile plug-and-play module that enhances existing baseline models' temporal stability and accuracy in online HD mapping, providing an effective auxiliary training strategy for improving temporal consistency without adding inference cost.

title: Innocent Panels, Hateful Stories: Evaluating and Detecting Hateful Intent in Multi-Turn Visual Story Generation
summary: Picture books and comics have long been used to disseminate hateful narratives because they are easily understood even by children, as exemplified by the notorious Nazi propaganda picture book \emph{Der Giftpilz}. Recently, frontier text-to-image (T2I) systems such as Gemini and GPT-Image have enabled conversational generation with consistent characters and scenes across turns, making hateful visual stories, namely ordered image groups that collectively convey hateful narratives, cheap and scalable to produce. Although prior work has studied hateful content generation by T2I systems, it focuses on individual images, leaving group-level hateful meaning largely unexplored. We aim to address the gap. Concretely, we introduce \texttt{HatefulStoryPrompts}, comprising 330 multi-turn configurations from 55 hateful stories across two languages and three visual styles, and evaluate five frontier models over 4,950 attempts. Every model completes over 80\% of the stories, with the strongest reaching 99.0\%. We further evaluate existing moderation systems on \texttt{HatefulVisualStory}, a human-labeled dataset of 969 hateful image sets and 990 benign controls, and find that they frequently miss group-level hateful meaning: dedicated safety models achieve at most 34.9\% recall, while a strong vision-language model reaches 67.5\%. Finally, we propose complementary proactive and post-generation defenses. An interaction-aware monitor achieves 97.3\% recall for prompt-only sessions and 92.6\% when the user supplies the first image, while post-generation methods jointly analyzing completed image groups reach 80.2\%. Our work shows that, as image generation evolves from isolated outputs to coherent visual narratives, safety must evolve accordingly, from per-image moderation to stateful reasoning over interactions and image relationships.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HatefulStoryPrompts, a benchmark of 330 multi-turn configurations from 55 hateful visual stories across two languages and three visual styles, revealing that five frontier T2I models complete over 80% of hateful stories (up to 99.0%). Existing moderation systems frequently miss group-level hateful meaning (max 67.5% recall), while proposed defenses achieve significantly better results: an interaction-aware monitor reaches 97.3% recall for prompt-only sessions and 92.6% with user images, and post-generation joint analysis reaches 80.2%.
AI.motivation: Prior work on hateful content generation by text-to-image (T2I) systems focuses on individual images, leaving group-level hateful meaning—where ordered image groups collectively convey hateful narratives—largely unexplored. Since frontier T2I systems now enable cheap, scalable production of hateful visual stories via conversational generation with consistent characters and scenes, this gap poses a significant safety concern that needs addressing.
AI.method: The authors construct HatefulStoryPrompts (330 multi-turn configurations from 55 hateful stories across two languages and three visual styles) and evaluate five frontier models over 4,950 attempts. They build HatefulVisualStory, a human-labeled dataset of 969 hateful image sets and 990 benign controls, to evaluate existing moderation systems. They also propose proactive defenses (an interaction-aware monitor) and post-generation defenses (joint analysis of completed image groups).
AI.result: Every tested T2I model completes over 80% of hateful stories, with the strongest reaching 99.0%. Existing moderation systems frequently miss group-level hateful meaning: dedicated safety models achieve at most 34.9% recall, while a strong vision-language model reaches 67.5%. The proposed interaction-aware monitor achieves 97.3% recall for prompt-only sessions and 92.6% when the user supplies the first image; post-generation joint analysis reaches 80.2%.
AI.conclusion: As image generation evolves from isolated outputs to coherent visual narratives, safety must evolve accordingly—from per-image moderation to stateful reasoning over interactions and image relationships. The proposed defenses demonstrate that group-level hateful meaning can be substantially better detected than with existing moderation systems.

title: StyleComposer: Training-Free Multi-Reference Style Composition
summary: The style of a painting is not monolithic: color, texture, and structure may come from different sources. Existing reference-guided methods transfer them as one style signal, leaving each attribute's source and strength outside the user's control. We ask where in a diffusion model one attribute can change while the others hold, and find that no single representation isolates all three. The proposed StyleComposer therefore routes each style attribute through the representation where it separates best and coordinates the routes over denoising time. Without training or inversion, it satisfies three references and the prompt jointly more closely than prior methods, and exposes one strength slider per attribute. Project page: https://lexxsh.github.io/StyleComposer

AI.tldr: StyleComposer is a training-free method that decomposes artistic style into color, texture, and structure attributes, routing each through the diffusion model representation where it separates best, and coordinating these routes over denoising time to enable independent control of multiple style references simultaneously.
AI.motivation: Existing reference-guided style transfer treats style as a monolithic signal, preventing users from independently controlling individual style attributes (color, texture, structure) and their strengths when combining multiple references.
AI.method: StyleComposer identifies which diffusion model representation best isolates each style attribute, routes each attribute through its optimal representation, and coordinates these separate routes across denoising timesteps—all without training or inversion.
AI.result: The method satisfies three style references and a text prompt jointly more closely than prior approaches, while additionally providing a per-attribute strength slider for user control.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling style into attributes and routing each through its best-separating representation enables finer-grained, user-controllable multi-reference style transfer in diffusion models without requiring training.

title: NeuroAdaptTrainer: A Fiji/ImageJ Plugin for YOLO-Based Neuron Segmentation, InteractiveCorrection and Transfer Learning
summary: Neuron counting and segmentation in microscopy images of neuronal cultures is a routine and time-consuming task in neuroscience research, traditionally performed through manual inspection or semi-automatic tools. We present NeuroAdaptTrainer, an open-source Fiji/ImageJ plugin that integrates a YOLO instance-segmentation model directly into the microscopist's workflow. The plugin allows a user to run automatic neuron detection on a single image or a batch of images, manually correct the resulting detections from within Fiji, and use those corrections to adapt the model to new imaging conditions via transfer learning. A built-in external validation module allows the base and adapted models to be compared quantitatively on a held-out annotated set. NeuroAdaptTrainer lowers the barrier for non-specialist users to benefit from deep-learning-based segmentation while keeping expert supervision at the center of the workflow.

AI.tldr: NeuroAdaptTrainer is an open-source Fiji/ImageJ plugin integrating YOLO instance-segmentation for automatic neuron counting, enabling manual correction, transfer-learning-based adaptation to new imaging conditions, and quantitative model validation all within a microscopist's workflow.
AI.motivation: Neuron counting and segmentation from microscopy images is routine yet time-consuming, traditionally relying on manual inspection or semi-automatic tools, and deep-learning methods are often inaccessible to non-specialist users.
AI.method: The plugin integrates a YOLO instance-segmentation model into Fiji/ImageJ, supports single or batch image processing, allows manual correction of detections in Fiji, uses those corrections for transfer-learning model adaptation, and includes an external validation module to quantitatively compare base and adapted models on a held-out annotated set.
AI.result: The plugin enables automatic neuron detection, user-driven model refinement via transfer learning, and quantitative benchmarking of adapted versus base models directly within the microscopy workflow.
AI.conclusion: NeuroAdaptTrainer reduces the barrier for non-specialist users to leverage deep-learning segmentation while keeping expert supervision central to the process.

title: In-Context Forcing: Uncovering Context Effects in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
summary: Current few-step autoregressive video diffusion models depend on previous fully denoised clean frames as context for all denoising steps of the current frame. However, these clean frames leak excessive local details, which causes the model to take shortcuts, resulting in compromised temporal semantics and dynamics. Inspired by the perspective of diffusion as masking, we explore the impact of noisy contexts on few-step autoregressive generation. Yet, simply applying contexts with the same noise levels provides insufficient guidance, leading to poor temporal consistency. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce In-Context Forcing, a progressive autoregressive paradigm that utilizes contexts with decreasing noise levels. By applying less masking to distant frames and more masking to adjacent ones, this approach provides adaptive guidance, effectively ensuring both robust temporal consistency and high inter-frame dynamics. Furthermore, by decoupling the strict dependence on previous clean frames, our paradigm enables cross-frame parallel denoising, achieving substantial inference acceleration without sacrificing performance. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both visual fidelity and inference speed.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces In-Context Forcing, a progressive autoregressive paradigm for few-step video diffusion models that uses contexts with decreasing noise levels instead of fully clean frames. By applying less masking to distant frames and more masking to adjacent ones, it provides adaptive guidance that improves temporal consistency and inter-frame dynamics while enabling cross-frame parallel denoising for faster inference.
AI.motivation: Current few-step autoregressive video diffusion models rely on fully denoised clean frames as context, but these leak excessive local details that cause the model to take shortcuts, compromising temporal semantics and dynamics. Using contexts with the same noise levels provides insufficient guidance, leading to poor temporal consistency.
AI.method: The proposed In-Context Forcing paradigm progressively uses contexts with decreasing noise levels—applying less masking to distant frames and more masking to adjacent frames—to provide adaptive guidance. It also decouples strict dependence on previous clean frames, enabling cross-frame parallel denoising.
AI.result: Experiments on VBench demonstrate that the method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both visual fidelity and inference speed, achieving substantial inference acceleration without sacrificing performance.
AI.conclusion: In-Context Forcing effectively resolves the dilemma between noisy and clean contexts in autoregressive video diffusion, providing robust temporal consistency, high inter-frame dynamics, and faster inference.

title: Grad-CAM for Vision Transformers: A Systematic Taxonomy and Audit of Methodological Ambiguity in Explainable AI
summary: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is widely used to visualize model decisions, but it was originally formulated for convolutional neural networks, where spatial feature maps and channel dimensions have clear architectural meanings. Vision Transformers (ViTs) do not provide the same structure, instead representing images through tokens, attention, residual streams, and multimodal interactions. This paper presents a systematic taxonomy and literature audit of how Grad-CAM and related methods are adapted, justified, and reported for ViT-based architectures. From an initial search of more than 550 papers, we identify 175 papers that apply Grad-CAM or Grad-CAM-adjacent methods to ViTs. We find that most papers do not provide a full mathematical or implementation-level account of how Grad-CAM is adapted to transformer representations. To characterize this gap, we introduce a descriptive taxonomy of ViT Grad-CAM adaptations that makes explicit the feature locations, gradient targets, spatial reconstruction steps, and aggregation choices that are often left implicit. This taxonomy is not intended to prescribe a single correct adaptation, but to clarify the range of methodological choices being made. The study shows that Grad-CAM on ViTs is often treated as a trivial extension of CNN-based Grad-CAM, despite requiring nontrivial choices that affect rigor, reproducibility, and interpretation.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically audits how Grad-CAM and related visualization methods are adapted to Vision Transformers (ViTs). From over 550 initial papers, 175 were identified as applying Grad-CAM to ViTs. The authors find that most works lack full mathematical or implementation-level details of their adaptations, and introduce a descriptive taxonomy clarifying the often-implicit choices involving feature locations, gradient targets, spatial reconstruction, and aggregation.
AI.motivation: Grad-CAM was originally designed for CNNs, where spatial feature maps and channels have clear architectural meanings. Vision Transformers lack this structure, yet Grad-CAM is widely applied to ViTs without explicit accounting for how the method is adapted, raising concerns about rigor, reproducibility, and interpretability.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic literature audit, screening over 550 papers and selecting 175 that apply Grad-CAM or Grad-CAM-adjacent methods to ViTs. They analyze these papers for completeness of adaptation details and introduce a descriptive taxonomy that makes explicit the feature locations, gradient targets, spatial reconstruction steps, and aggregation choices used in ViT Grad-CAM adaptations.
AI.result: Most papers do not provide a full mathematical or implementation-level account of how Grad-CAM is adapted to transformer representations. Grad-CAM on ViTs is frequently treated as a trivial extension of the CNN version despite requiring nontrivial methodological choices that affect rigor, reproducibility, and interpretation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed taxonomy is not intended to prescribe a single correct adaptation but to clarify the range of methodological choices being made, enabling more rigorous and reproducible use of Grad-CAM on ViTs.

title: A Paragraph is Worth a Thousand Captions: Rethinking Text Supervision for Vision-Language Retrieval
comment: Accepted at the MUCG workshop, ECCV 2026
summary: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP and BLIP are typically trained on short image captions, limiting their ability to retrieve images from detailed textual descriptions. While methods such as Long-CLIP extend the token limit through positional embedding interpolation, we ask a simpler question: does training text granularity alone determine long-text retrieval performance? We present a systematic study of supervision ranging from single captions to multi-sentence paragraphs for contrastive image-text retrieval. Using a synthetic pipeline based on Qwen2-VL and Llama 3.2 Vision, we generate diverse captions, hard negatives, and quality-scored paragraphs for 500K CC3M images. To isolate the effect of text granularity, we fine-tune only the BLIP text encoder while keeping the vision encoder frozen across 10 training configurations. Our paragraph-supervised models match Long-CLIP-L on ShareGPT4V and outperform it by more than 14 points on DOCCI for image-to-text retrieval, without architectural changes. We further show that paragraph supervision enables effective use of long token sequences, whereas caption-only training degrades beyond 60 tokens. Increasing caption diversity improves short-caption retrieval with diminishing returns, while paragraph supervision consistently benefits long-description benchmarks and hard negatives prove detrimental in text-only fine-tuning. Evaluations on Flickr30k, COCO, ShareGPT4V, and DOCCI provide a comprehensive analysis of the trade-offs between text granularity, retrieval direction, and description length.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically studies whether training text granularity alone determines long-text retrieval performance in contrastive vision-language models. Using a synthetic pipeline with Qwen2-VL and Llama 3.2 Vision to generate diverse captions, hard negatives, and quality-scored paragraphs for 500K CC3M images, the authors fine-tune only the BLIP text encoder across 10 configurations. Paragraph-supervised models match Long-CLIP-L on ShareGPT4V and outperform it by 14+ points on DOCCI without architectural changes, showing that text granularity is a critical factor.
AI.motivation: Contrastive vision-language models (CLIP, BLIP) are limited by short image captions, restricting their ability to retrieve images from detailed textual descriptions. While prior work addresses this via architectural changes (e.g., positional embedding interpolation in Long-CLIP), the paper investigates whether training text granularity alone determines long-text retrieval performance.
AI.method: The authors create a synthetic data pipeline using Qwen2-VL and Llama 3.2 Vision to generate diverse captions, hard negatives, and quality-scored paragraphs for 500K CC3M images. They isolate the effect of text granularity by fine-tuning only the BLIP text encoder while keeping the vision encoder frozen across 10 training configurations, ranging from single captions to multi-sentence paragraphs.
AI.result: Paragraph-supervised models match Long-CLIP-L on ShareGPT4V and outperform it by more than 14 points on DOCCI for image-to-text retrieval without architectural changes. Paragraph supervision enables effective use of long token sequences, while caption-only training degrades beyond 60 tokens. Increasing caption diversity improves short-caption retrieval with diminishing returns, and hard negatives prove detrimental in text-only fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Training text granularity is a decisive factor for long-text retrieval performance. Paragraph supervision can match or exceed architectural modifications like Long-CLIP, while caption diversity helps short-caption retrieval and hard negatives are counterproductive in text-only fine-tuning. Evaluations on Flickr30k, COCO, ShareGPT4V, and DOCCI provide a comprehensive understanding of trade-offs between text granularity, retrieval direction, and description length.

title: Context Matters: Support Set Selection and Failure Detection for In-Context Medical Image Segmentation
summary: In-context learning (ICL) adapts medical image segmentation models to unseen structures and modalities without retraining by conditioning on a task-specific support set of image-mask exemplars. Because this support set is the model's only task-specific signal, its composition directly influences segmentation performance. In this work, we investigate the support set as a controllable determinant of ICL reliability. First, we compare random sampling against similarity-based selection, where exemplars are retrieved based on their visual similarity to the query image. Second, we train a transformer-based classifier to predict, from the query and support images alone, whether a segmentation will fall below a specified Intersection-over-Union (IoU) threshold. Using MultiverSeg with DINOv3 embeddings across four benchmarks and three imaging modalities, we show that similarity-based selection consistently matches or outperforms random sampling, with the largest gains at the smallest support set sizes. Furthermore, our classifier predicts segmentation failure above chance on all four benchmarks. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that the reliability of in-context segmentation can be both improved via informed support selection and anticipated before use, providing practical mechanisms for safer clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the support set composition affects the reliability of in-context learning (ICL) for medical image segmentation. The authors compare random vs. similarity-based exemplar selection and train a transformer classifier to predict segmentation failure (IoU below a threshold) before deployment. Using MultiverSeg with DINOv3 embeddings across four benchmarks and three imaging modalities, they find similarity-based selection matches or outperforms random sampling (especially with small support sets), and the failure predictor works above chance across all benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The support set is the only task-specific signal in ICL for medical image segmentation, so its composition directly influences performance. However, how to control this set to make ICL more reliable—and whether failures can be anticipated—has not been systematically investigated.
AI.method: The authors (1) compare random support set sampling against similarity-based retrieval using visual similarity (DINOv3 embeddings) to the query image, and (2) train a transformer-based classifier that takes query and support images as input to predict whether the segmentation will fall below a specified IoU threshold. Experiments use MultiverSeg across four benchmarks and three imaging modalities.
AI.result: Similarity-based support selection consistently matches or outperforms random sampling, with the largest gains at the smallest support set sizes. The transformer-based failure predictor performs above chance on all four benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: In-context segmentation reliability can be improved via informed support selection and anticipated before use, providing practical mechanisms for safer clinical deployment.

title: Positive-Unlabeled Preference Optimization For Chest X-ray Report Generation
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for radiology report generation are typically trained on retrospective clinical reports, which suffer from omission noise: clinically present findings are left unreported due to the omission of subtle findings. For example, prior studies show that cardiomegaly may be omitted from ICU chest X-ray reports when the imaging request is focused on monitoring support device placement. As a result, models trained with standard approaches inherit these omissions, learning to under-report findings themselves. We propose PU-DPO, a preference optimization framework to prevent omission noise from corrupting the preference signal. We reformulate the objective under a positive-unlabeled (PU) learning framework, treating absent mentions as unlabeled rather than truly negative. Our framework provides preference supervision using constructed contrastive pairs, generated using edits to model responses, producing variants that explicitly mention or omit a specific finding. Generated responses that mention the finding are naturally preferred in the context of visual evidence. Across semi-synthetic experiments and analyses on real-world chest radiograph benchmarks where adjudicated labels are available, PU-DPO yields consistent gains in detection rates and recovery of hidden positives across multiple pathologies, and is more robust to omission noise than prior approaches.

AI.tldr: PU-DPO is a preference optimization framework for radiology report generation that reformulates the training objective under positive-unlabeled (PU) learning to prevent omission noise (clinically present findings left unreported) from corrupting the preference signal, using contrastive pairs that explicitly mention or omit specific findings.
AI.motivation: VLMs for radiology report generation are trained on retrospective clinical reports that suffer from omission noise—clinically present findings are left unreported (e.g., cardiomegaly may be omitted from ICU chest X-ray reports when the imaging request focuses on device placement monitoring). Models trained with standard approaches inherit these omissions and learn to under-report findings themselves.
AI.method: PU-DPO reformulates the preference optimization objective under a positive-unlabeled (PU) learning framework, treating absent mentions as unlabeled rather than truly negative. It provides preference supervision using constructed contrastive pairs generated via edits to model responses, producing variants that explicitly mention or omit a specific finding.
AI.result: Across semi-synthetic experiments and analyses on real-world chest radiograph benchmarks with adjudicated labels, PU-DPO yields consistent gains in detection rates and recovery of hidden positives across multiple pathologies, and is more robust to omission noise than prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: PU-DPO effectively mitigates omission noise corruption in preference signals for radiology report generation, improving detection of findings that are present but may be omitted in training data.

title: LoDA: A Level of Detection Aware Method and a Multimodal Sensing Benchmark for Object Level Change Detection
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026) Main Track
summary: High-definition 3D LiDAR maps are important for autonomous driving and smart-city services, which require reliable detection of object-level changes in multi-temporal urban LiDAR to keep digital maps aligned with the physical world. Existing approaches from raster height differencing to depth image and point-cloud networks often remain tile-based and threshold-driven, yielding per-point scores without explicit detection limits or consistent object-level labels. We propose an object-level 3D change-detection pipeline that integrates detection-limit-aware registration, geometry-driven object proxies with rule-based semantic and instance segmentation, and displacement cues in height, volume, and surface-normal direction to assign five change labels with confidence. By decoupling registration, geometry, and semantics, the pipeline propagates pose uncertainty into spatially varying detection limits, stabilizes cross-epoch correspondences, and suppresses false changes caused by residual misalignment and density variation. We also present LoDA, a level-of-detection (LoD) aware benchmark for the Subiaco district with fused multi-temporal vehicle-LiDAR maps constructed with LiDAR, GNSS, and IMU support, semantic instances, and object-level annotations. On this benchmark, our method achieves 95.0% accuracy, 90.8% macro F1, and 83.0% macro IoU, exceeding the best baseline by 8.7 IoU points and 4.4 F1 points. On the public Urb3DCD-V2 benchmark evaluated under the official point-wise protocol, it reaches 96.81% mean accuracy and 89.52% mean change IoU, improving over the strongest reported baselines by 1.36 points in mAcc and 3.18 points in mIoUch.

AI.tldr: A novel object-level 3D change-detection pipeline for multi-temporal urban LiDAR maps that integrates detection-limit-aware registration, geometry-driven object proxies, and rule-based semantic/instance segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results on a new LoDA benchmark and the public Urb3DCD-V2.
AI.motivation: High-definition 3D LiDAR maps need reliable object-level change detection to stay aligned with the physical world, but existing methods (raster height differencing, depth image, point-cloud networks) are tile-based, threshold-driven, and produce per-point scores without explicit detection limits or consistent object-level labels.
AI.method: The pipeline decouples registration, geometry, and semantics: (1) detection-limit-aware registration propagates pose uncertainty into spatially varying detection limits; (2) geometry-driven object proxies with rule-based semantic and instance segmentation stabilize cross-epoch correspondences; (3) displacement cues in height, volume, and surface-normal direction assign five change labels with confidence, suppressing false changes from residual misalignment and density variation. A new LoDA benchmark with fused multi-temporal vehicle-LiDAR maps is also introduced.
AI.result: On LoDA benchmark: 95.0% accuracy, 90.8% macro F1, 83.0% macro IoU (besting baselines by 8.7 IoU and 4.4 F1 points). On Urb3DCD-V2 under official point-wise protocol: 96.81% mAcc and 89.52% mIoUch, improving over strongest baselines by 1.36 mAcc and 3.18 mIoUch points.
AI.conclusion: The decoupled detection-limit-aware pipeline with explicit object-level labels provides reliable and consistent 3D change detection, outperforming existing baselines and establishing a new benchmark for LoD-aware evaluation.

title: Text-Guided Refinement of Multi-sequence Glioma Subregion Segmentation with a Vision-Language Foundation Model
summary:
Background: Accurate glioma subregion delineation is important for radiotherapy planning and longitudinal monitoring, but manual contour correction is time-consuming. Models such as nnU-Net may generalize imperfectly and lack clinician-directed text correction.
  Purpose: We investigated adapting a three-dimensional (3D) vision-language foundation model for text-guided brain tumor segmentation refinement.
  Methods: We developed a lightweight VoxTell-based framework. Pretrained VoxTell generated initial masks. Oracle prompts derived from segmentation errors encoded target, action, location, imaging evidence, edit size, and preservation constraints. Frozen Qwen/VoxTell prompt embeddings were injected through trainable projections into its multiscale decoder conditioning; other weights remained frozen. Training, validation, and testing used 901, 100, and 250 BraTS-GLI cases. Cross-dataset transfer was evaluated on 100 meningioma, metastasis, pediatric tumor, and UPENN-GBM cases.
  Results: On the internal test set using post-contrast T1-weighted input, correct instructions improved subregion Dice similarity coefficient (DSC; enhancing tumor, edema, and necrotic/non-enhancing core) from $0.774\pm0.158$ to $0.796\pm0.137$. They outperformed blank prompts ($0.762\pm0.155$; Holm-adjusted $p<0.001$, $d_z=0.71$) and contradictory prompts ($0.770\pm0.163$; $p<0.001$, $d_z=0.48$). In cross-dataset testing, correct instructions improved DSC from $0.527\pm0.287$ to $0.550\pm0.278$ and outperformed contradictory instructions ($0.504\pm0.275$; $p<0.001$, $d_z=0.43$).
  Conclusion: A 3D vision-language foundation model can perform instruction-guided refinement of glioma subregion segmentations. Sensitivity to correct, blank, and contradictory prompts suggests text-dependent contour editing rather than nonspecific post-processing, supporting further evaluation as a clinician-in-the-loop tool.

AI.tldr: This paper presents VoxTell, a lightweight 3D vision-language foundation model framework for text-guided refinement of brain tumor subregion segmentation. By injecting text embeddings from correct, blank, or contradictory clinician-style prompts into a frozen pretrained segmentation decoder, they demonstrate instruction-dependent improvements in Dice similarity coefficients on both internal (BraTS-GLI) and cross-dataset tests.
AI.motivation: Accurate glioma subregion delineation is critical for radiotherapy and monitoring, but manual contour correction is time-consuming. Existing models like nnU-Net generalize imperfectly and lack the ability to incorporate clinician-directed text corrections for segmentation refinement.
AI.method: A VoxTell-based framework was developed where a pretrained 3D vision-language model generates initial masks. Oracle prompts encoding target, action, location, imaging evidence, edit size, and preservation constraints were derived from segmentation errors. Frozen Qwen/VoxTell prompt embeddings were injected via trainable projections into the multiscale decoder, with all other weights frozen. The model was trained on 901 BraTS-GLI cases and tested on 250 internal plus 100 cross-dataset cases.
AI.result: On internal testing with post-contrast T1-weighted input, correct instructions improved DSC from 0.774 to 0.796, outperforming blank prompts (0.762, p<0.001) and contradictory prompts (0.770, p<0.001). Cross-dataset testing showed correct instructions improved DSC from 0.527 to 0.550 and outperformed contradictory instructions (0.504, p<0.001).
AI.conclusion: A 3D vision-language foundation model can perform instruction-guided refinement of glioma subregion segmentations. The sensitivity to different prompt types confirms text-dependent contour editing rather than nonspecific post-processing, supporting further evaluation as a clinician-in-the-loop tool.

title: Adapting Vision Foundation Models with Cascaded Semantics
comment: Accepted by Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. Project page: https://xixiaouab.github.io/Cascaded-Semantics/
summary: Prompt tuning, a leading parameter-efficient adaptation paradigm in NLP, has recently been extended to computer vision. Visual prompt tuning (VPT) adapts pre-trained vision transformers (ViTs) by updating a small set of additional prompt parameters. However, existing visual prompts are randomly initialized and do not exploit prior knowledge, such as instructions in NLP. We address this gap by injecting two complementary semantic priors into VPT. Fundamental image priors, including color, texture, and shape, are extracted with classical hand-crafted operators and injected into the input space, while self-attention maps provide instance-aware semantics in the feature space. We further propose a cascaded scheme that integrates both priors throughout ViT adaptation. Experiments on 34 challenging image classification datasets demonstrate superior downstream adaptation while tuning only 0.74% of ViT parameters. Project page: https://xixiaouab.github.io/Cascaded-Semantics/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Cascaded Semantics for Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT), injecting two complementary semantic priors—hand-crafted image priors (color, texture, shape) in the input space and self-attention map priors in the feature space—through a cascaded scheme to improve ViT adaptation. It achieves superior performance on 34 image classification datasets while tuning only 0.74% of ViT parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing visual prompts in VPT are randomly initialized and do not leverage prior knowledge (unlike NLP prompts that exploit instructions). The paper addresses this gap by injecting semantic priors into visual prompt tuning.
AI.method: The method injects two complementary semantic priors: (1) fundamental image priors (color, texture, shape) extracted via classical hand-crafted operators in the input space, and (2) self-attention maps providing instance-aware semantics in the feature space. A cascaded scheme integrates both priors throughout the ViT adaptation process.
AI.result: Experiments on 34 challenging image classification datasets demonstrate superior downstream adaptation performance while tuning only 0.74% of ViT parameters.
AI.conclusion: Injecting cascaded semantic priors (both hand-crafted image priors and self-attention map priors) into visual prompt tuning significantly improves downstream adaptation efficiency and effectiveness over random initialization.

title: Invisible Shortcuts: Why Vision Encoders Know Your Camera
summary: Deep vision models exploit shortcuts, relying on cues that correlate with supervision signals. Prior work has focused on visible biases, such as object-background or texture correlations. We identify a different source of shortcut learning: invisible metadata traces embedded at the pixel level, for metadata such as image processing and photo acquisition. We hypothesize that large-scale semantic supervision, whether through categorical labels (ImageNet) or billion-scale captions (LAION), naturally induces metadata-semantics correlations during pretraining, leading models to convert low-level signals into predictive features. By introducing controlled metadata-semantics correlations, we show that stronger ones produce systematically higher sensitivity to metadata traces and larger performance degradation under metadata distribution shifts. We further explore mitigation strategies applied during and after pretraining that reduce sensitivity not only to targeted metadata but also to unseen ones, without sacrificing performance on downstream tasks. Metadata sensitivity also has a positive side: it partly explains the strong generated-image detection ability of some encoders, while its mitigation can improve out-of-distribution generalization. Code: https://github.com/ryan-caesar-ramos/visual-encoder-traces

AI.tldr: This paper identifies invisible metadata traces (e.g., image processing and photo acquisition cues) embedded at the pixel level as a source of shortcut learning in deep vision models. Large-scale semantic supervision induces metadata-semantics correlations during pretraining, causing models to exploit these low-level signals as predictive features. Stronger metadata-semantics correlations lead to higher sensitivity to metadata traces and greater performance degradation under metadata distribution shifts. The authors propose mitigation strategies that reduce sensitivity to both targeted and unseen metadata without harming downstream performance. Metadata sensitivity also explains some encoders' strong generated-image detection ability, and mitigation can improve out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.motivation: Prior work on shortcut learning in vision models has focused on visible biases like object-background or texture correlations, but has overlooked invisible metadata traces embedded at the pixel level. The authors aim to identify and characterize this previously underexplored source of shortcut learning.
AI.method: The authors introduce controlled metadata-semantics correlations during pretraining to systematically study how large-scale semantic supervision (categorical labels from ImageNet or captions from LAION) induces metadata sensitivity. They explore mitigation strategies applied both during and after pretraining to reduce sensitivity to targeted and unseen metadata traces.
AI.result: Stronger metadata-semantics correlations produce systematically higher sensitivity to metadata traces and larger performance degradation under metadata distribution shifts. The proposed mitigation strategies reduce sensitivity to both targeted and unseen metadata without sacrificing downstream performance. Metadata sensitivity also partially explains strong generated-image detection in some encoders.
AI.conclusion: Invisible metadata traces are a significant and previously underappreciated source of shortcut learning in deep vision models. These traces can be mitigated effectively, and doing so can improve out-of-distribution generalization, while also providing insights into generated-image detection capabilities.

title: MOSAIK: Multi-Patch Content-Aware Spatial Allocation of Image Tokens for Efficient Generation
summary: Pixel-space diffusion models avoid the reconstruction ceiling of latent diffusion models by generating directly in image space. However, their substantially higher token count makes generation expensive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Several existing efficiency methods reduce this cost by using larger patches at selected denoising steps, thereby representing the image with fewer tokens. Yet, each step still uses a single patch size uniformly across the entire image, overlooking that different regions suffer different fidelity losses when coarsened. We introduce MOSAIK, a damage-guided framework that varies patch size across regions and denoising steps. MOSAIK adapts the PixelDiT backbone to generate arbitrary heterogeneous patch layouts, and a lightweight predictor uses intermediate denoising features to estimate the fidelity loss caused by coarsening each region. Given a token budget, our damage-guided layout predictor assigns fine patches to sensitive regions and coarse patches elsewhere. Remarkably, while reducing FLOPs by 70% and token count by 83%, MOSAIK matches the full-compute PixelDiT on GenEval and its DPG-Bench score drops by only 1.0 point. Compared to diverse efficiency paradigms, including temporal patch scheduling and feature caching, our approach delivers highly competitive performance at moderate budgets and consistently outperforms these baselines in highly constrained compute regimes.

AI.tldr: MOSAIK is a damage-guided framework for pixel-space diffusion models that varies patch sizes across image regions and denoising steps, reducing FLOPs by 70% and token count by 83% while matching full-compute PixelDiT performance on GenEval.
AI.motivation: Pixel-space diffusion models generate directly in image space but suffer from high computational costs due to quadratic self-attention complexity with high token counts. Existing efficiency methods use uniform patch sizes per step, overlooking that different image regions experience different fidelity losses when coarsened.
AI.method: MOSAIK adapts the PixelDiT backbone to generate arbitrary heterogeneous patch layouts and uses a lightweight predictor that leverages intermediate denoising features to estimate fidelity loss from coarsening each region. Under a token budget, the damage-guided layout predictor assigns fine patches to sensitive regions and coarse patches elsewhere.
AI.result: MOSAIK reduces FLOPs by 70% and token count by 83% while matching full-compute PixelDiT on GenEval, with only a 1.0 point drop on DPG-Bench. It outperforms temporal patch scheduling and feature caching baselines, especially in highly constrained compute regimes.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, damage-guided patch sizing across regions and steps is a highly effective efficiency strategy for pixel-space diffusion models, delivering competitive quality at significantly reduced computational cost compared to existing efficiency paradigms.

title: CDSeg: A Renderable Gaussian Carrier for Image-to-3D Label Transfer
summary: Modern image models provide strong cues about \emph{what} should be segmented in each view, but their masks do not by themselves determine \emph{where} those labels should persist in 3D. We present Cross-Domain Segmentation via Gaussian Splatting (CDSeg), a label-transfer interface that requires no task-specific 3D segmentation training and uses Gaussian primitives as a renderable label carrier. An external mask source supplies the labels, while renderer-derived visibility determines which 3D primitives receive them. The carrier is instantiated either by completing each input point into one Gaussian, preserving its index, or by reusing the native primitives of an optimized Gaussian scene. CDSeg records pixel--primitive associations during rendering and fuses multi-view masks through voting and a local filter. The resulting labels can be returned to the original points, retained on the native Gaussian scene, or rendered into other views. CDSeg covers promptable, automatic instance, semantic, and LiDAR settings and processes scenes with millions of primitives in seconds. It obtains 92.35\% mIoU on DesktopObjects-360, 95.89\% on NeRDS-360, and 65.77\% on the full ScanNet-v2 validation split using the provided 2D semantic annotations. CDSeg thereby provides one interface for reusing 2D masks across point clouds, Gaussian scenes, and image views without a task-specific 3D segmentation network.

AI.tldr: CDSeg is a label-transfer interface that uses Gaussian splatting primitives as renderable label carriers to transfer 2D masks from external sources into 3D, without requiring task-specific 3D segmentation training. It works across point clouds, Gaussian scenes, and image views, achieving high mIoU scores on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Modern image models produce strong 2D segmentation cues but determining where those labels persist in 3D remains a challenge. Existing approaches typically require task-specific 3D segmentation training, which is expensive and not generalizable across domains.
AI.method: CDSeg uses Gaussian primitives as renderable label carriers. An external mask source supplies 2D labels, while renderer-derived visibility determines which 3D primitives receive them. The carrier is instantiated either by completing each input point into one Gaussian (preserving its index) or by reusing native primitives of an optimized Gaussian scene. Pixel-primitive associations are recorded during rendering, and multi-view masks are fused through voting and a local filter. Labels can be returned to original points, retained on Gaussian scenes, or rendered into other views.
AI.result: CDSeg achieves 92.35% mIoU on DesktopObjects-360, 95.89% on NeRDS-360, and 65.77% on the full ScanNet-v2 validation split. It processes scenes with millions of primitives in seconds and covers promptable, automatic instance, semantic, and LiDAR settings.
AI.conclusion: CDSeg provides a single interface for reusing 2D masks across point clouds, Gaussian scenes, and image views without needing a task-specific 3D segmentation network, making it a versatile and efficient cross-domain label-transfer solution.

title: VideoArgus: Agentic Rubric-Grounded Unified Evaluation for Video Generation and Editing
summary: Evaluating generated videos remains challenging because existing benchmarks rely on fixed evaluation content, cover only a subset of generation and editing settings, and provide limited evidence for their scores. We introduce VideoArgus, a unified rubric-grounded framework covering five video generation and editing settings. For each input instance, VideoArgus generates an output-blind, sample-specific rubric once and reuses it to evaluate all corresponding candidate videos. The rubric defines concrete criteria, scoring rules, failure modes, and evidence plans, which guide criterion-specific VLM QA and visual tools to produce evidence-grounded criterion scores, rationales, and a diagnostic report. We further construct VideoArgus-Bench, containing 1,026 curated input instances built from 653 high-quality images and 416 high-quality videos, with all benchmark rubrics pre-generated, frozen, and released. On a separate 1,260-video human-alignment set, VideoArgus achieves higher within-input Spearman and Kendall correlations with human judgments than the corresponding benchmark-specific evaluators across all five tasks. Model rankings also remain largely consistent across different rubric-generation and evaluation-VLM backbones. All code and data are released. Visit our project page: https://zzzmyyzeng.github.io/VideoArgus

AI.tldr: VideoArgus is a unified rubric-grounded evaluation framework for video generation and editing, covering five settings. It generates output-blind, sample-specific rubrics reused across candidate videos, guiding VLM QA and visual tools for evidence-grounded scoring. VideoArgus-Bench includes 1,026 curated input instances, and the framework achieves higher human alignment than task-specific evaluators on all five tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing video evaluation benchmarks rely on fixed content, cover only a subset of generation/editing settings, and provide limited evidence supporting their scores, motivating a more unified and evidence-grounded framework.
AI.method: VideoArgus generates an output-blind, sample-specific rubric per input instance, reused across all candidate videos. Rubrics define criteria, scoring rules, failure modes, and evidence plans, which guide criterion-specific VLM QA and visual tools to produce evidence-grounded scores, rationales, and diagnostic reports. VideoArgus-Bench comprises 1,026 curated inputs from 653 images and 416 videos with pre-generated frozen rubrics.
AI.result: On a 1,260-video human-alignment set, VideoArgus achieves higher within-input Spearman and Kendall correlations with human judgments than benchmark-specific evaluators across all five tasks. Model rankings remain consistent across different rubric-generation and evaluation-VLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: VideoArgus provides a unified, rubric-grounded, and evidence-based evaluation approach that improves human alignment across multiple video generation and editing tasks, with all code and data released.

title: APQF: Agentic Profiling-Guided Structured Pruning and Mixed-Precision Quantization with Adaptive Fine-Tuning
summary: Modern deep neural networks achieve strong performance, but their scale makes them costly and slow, especially on resource-constrained edge devices. Pruning and quantization address this, but rely on manual, expert choices and on algorithms that are hard to apply across architectures. Uniform settings also ignore how differently individual layers respond to compression, which costs accuracy. We introduce APQF, an agentic profiling-guided framework that combines structured pruning, mixed-precision quantization-aware training, and accuracy recovery in one automated pipeline. A profiling agent measures how cost is distributed across the model and how sensitive each part is to pruning, and this evidence drives per-layer pruning ratios, per-layer bit-widths, and the recovery strategy, all proposed by LLM planners and validated before execution. To our knowledge, APQF is the first framework to combine LLM-guided, profiling-grounded decisions with a fully training-aware pruning and quantization pipeline for both CNNs and vision transformers. We evaluate APQF on ResNet, VGG7, ViT, DeiT, and Swin using ImageNet-1k and CIFAR-10. On ImageNet it cuts compute to 5.6-7.7 percent of the original bit-operations, a 13-18x reduction, while keeping accuracy close to the baseline, and under a 200K-image budget it stays roughly 17 points higher in Top-1 than existing joint pruning and quantization methods. On CIFAR-10 it compresses further than that method on four of five architectures. On VGG7 it reaches 93.15 percent using only 0.41 percent of baseline bit-operations, the only method at that compression level to improve on its full-precision baseline. Ablations show that uniform compression loses the most accuracy at matched compute, and that withholding profiling data from the planner hurts every model. Six LLM planners, including free open-weight ones, all reach 97.4-97.9 percent on Swin-Tiny.

AI.tldr: APQF is an agentic profiling-guided framework that combines structured pruning, mixed-precision quantization-aware training, and accuracy recovery into one automated pipeline, using LLM planners guided by profiling evidence to make per-layer compression decisions. It achieves 13-18x compute reduction on ImageNet while maintaining accuracy, and outperforms existing joint pruning and quantization methods across CNNs and vision transformers.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks are costly and slow on edge devices. Existing pruning and quantization methods rely on manual expert choices, are hard to apply across architectures, and uniform settings ignore how individual layers respond differently to compression, leading to accuracy loss.
AI.method: APQF uses a profiling agent to measure cost distribution and layer sensitivity to pruning. This evidence drives per-layer pruning ratios, per-layer bit-widths, and recovery strategy, all proposed by LLM planners and validated before execution. It combines LLM-guided, profiling-grounded decisions with a fully training-aware pruning and quantization pipeline for both CNNs and vision transformers.
AI.result: On ImageNet, APQF cuts compute to 5.6-7.7 percent of original bit-operations (13-18x reduction) with accuracy close to baseline, and stays ~17 points higher in Top-1 than existing methods under a 200K-image budget. On CIFAR-10 it compresses further on four of five architectures. On VGG7 it reaches 93.15% accuracy using only 0.41% of baseline bit-operations, improving on its full-precision baseline. Ablations show uniform compression loses most accuracy at matched compute, and removing profiling data hurts all models. Six LLM planners all achieve 97.4-97.9% on Swin-Tiny.
AI.conclusion: APQF demonstrates that combining LLM-driven planning with profiling-grounded evidence in a fully training-aware pipeline yields state-of-the-art compression results across diverse architectures, outperforming uniform compression and existing joint pruning-quantization methods while remaining robust to the choice of LLM planner.

title: DynaPix: Can Vision-Language Models Identify the Exact Future?
summary: Acting in a physical scene requires knowing its real later state, not a plausible one. Current evaluations often accept words or a realistic-looking image, so the predicted state is never checked against the true one. We introduce DynaPix (Dynamic Pixels), a benchmark that makes prediction checkable. Given a video clip that stops before a key event and a question about a later moment, a model must pick the true future image from close candidates or a large gallery. The scenes come from a physics simulator, so the correct image and its time are known exactly and the wrong options are deliberately similar. Models often succeed when a visible event marks the target moment, but are near chance when only elapsed time marks it. Gallery search is harder still, as the true image rarely ranks first. People handle the elapsed-time items well, so the difficulty lies with the models, not the questions. Training on scene accounts drawn from the simulator's true record, not a teacher's guess, repairs much of this but not the longer elapsed time case. DynaPix thus exposes a temporal-anchoring gap: models attach a prediction to an event far better than to time itself.

AI.tldr: DynaPix is a benchmark that evaluates visual prediction models by requiring them to select the true future image (from a physics simulator) from distractors, rather than merely generating plausible images or text. It reveals a "temporal-anchoring gap": models perform well when an event marks the target moment, but near chance when only elapsed time does; training on true simulator records helps but doesn't fully fix longer time spans.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of physical scene prediction accept plausible words or images and never verify the predicted state against the true one, so models are not actually held accountable for correct future states.
AI.method: DynaPix builds a benchmark from a physics simulator where the ground-truth future image and exact time are known. Models are given a video clip that stops before a key event and a question about a later moment, and must pick the true future image from either close candidates or a large gallery, with deliberately similar wrong options.
AI.result: Models succeed when a visible event marks the target moment but are near chance when only elapsed time marks it. Gallery search is harder, with the true image rarely ranking first. Humans handle elapsed-time items well. Training on simulator's true record repairs much of the gap but not the longer elapsed-time case.
AI.conclusion: DynaPix exposes a temporal-anchoring gap: models attach predictions to events far better than to time itself, indicating a fundamental weakness in temporal grounding for visual prediction.

title: HERA: Historical Evidence Routing Adapter for Physical Prediction in Latent World Models
summary: Predictive video models have emerged as promising world models by learning latent visual dynamics from large-scale video. Yet these models remain challenged by physical events under occlusion, where later predictions may depend on object evidence that is no longer available in the current view. Addressing this challenge requires historical evidence not only to be preserved but also to remain accessible when it becomes relevant to a subsequent prediction. Existing approaches mainly enlarge the temporal context, cache generic video features, or impose explicit object-centric states, thereby improving the capacity or structure of retained history. However, they do not directly address how relevant historical evidence can be selectively retrieved and integrated into a pretrained predictor without interfering with its native latent workspace. Accordingly, we introduce HERA (Historical Evidence Routing Adapter), a framework for routing retained historical evidence into a frozen latent predictor, and instantiate it with Register-Routed Patch Memory (RRPM), a lightweight adapter comprising a Structured Memory Bank, Memory Registers, and Workspace Registers. On the IntPhys2 Main split, HERA with RRPM improves the pairwise AvgSurprise accuracy of V-JEPA 2-G from 52.57% to 54.35%. Subgroup analysis shows particularly strong improvements on fixed-camera continuity, from 46.15% to 57.69%, and fixed-camera immutability, from 46.15% to 63.46%. These results support historical evidence routing as a practical adaptation strategy for physical prediction in latent world models.

AI.tldr: HERA (Historical Evidence Routing Adapter) is a framework that routes retained historical evidence into a frozen latent video predictor, instantiated with RRPM (Register-Routed Patch Memory). It improves physical prediction under occlusion on IntPhys2, boosting V-JEPA 2-G accuracy from 52.57% to 54.35%, with notable gains in fixed-camera continuity and immutability tasks.
AI.motivation: Predictive video models struggle with physical events under occlusion because later predictions may depend on object evidence no longer visible in the current view. Existing methods enlarge temporal context or cache generic features but fail to selectively retrieve and integrate relevant historical evidence into a pretrained predictor without disturbing its native latent workspace.
AI.method: HERA introduces a routing-based adapter that selectively retrieves and integrates relevant historical evidence into a frozen latent predictor. It is instantiated via RRPM, a lightweight adapter consisting of a Structured Memory Bank, Memory Registers, and Workspace Registers that route evidence without modifying the pretrained backbone.
AI.result: On IntPhys2 Main split, HERA with RRPM improves pairwise AvgSurprise accuracy of V-JEPA 2-G from 52.57% to 54.35%. Fixed-camera continuity improves from 46.15% to 57.69%, and fixed-camera immutability from 46.15% to 63.46%.
AI.conclusion: Historical evidence routing proves to be a practical and effective adaptation strategy for physical prediction in latent world models, particularly enhancing performance on occlusion-related tasks without interfering with the pretrained predictor.

title: OmniMech: All-in-one Multimodal Mechanical Benchmark for 3D Reconstruction
summary: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can generate executable CAD programs from images, but existing methods mainly target coarse, general-purpose 3D objects and rarely address the fine-grained geometry and millimeter-level tolerances required in industrial mechanical design. We introduce OmniMech, the first million-scale benchmark for evaluating VLMs on executable CAD generation from industrial manufacturing data. OmniMech contains more than 251,000 fully dimensioned and toleranced 2D orthographic drawings, paired with native CAD models, multi-view renderings, mesh, STEP and B-rep representations, and rich semantic annotations. The benchmark includes four tasks: (1) parametric CAD program synthesis from engineering drawings; (2) diagram-to-3D reasoning for geometrically and structurally consistent reconstruction; (3) annotation-grounded reasoning over dimensions, symbols, feature callouts, and manufacturing constraints; and (4) tool-augmented agentic reasoning using visualization, measurement, CAD execution, and verification tools. Experiments show that current VLMs and CAD-specialized models still struggle with executable program synthesis, fine-grained 3D reconstruction, and reliable enforcement of dimensions and tolerances. We will release the benchmark data, evaluation code, and tool interfaces to support future research.

AI.tldr: OmniMech is the first million-scale benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on executable CAD program generation from industrial manufacturing data, containing 251,000+ dimensioned 2D orthographic drawings paired with CAD models and multiple representations, spanning four tasks from parametric program synthesis to tool-augmented agentic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM-based CAD generation methods target coarse, general-purpose 3D objects and fail to address the fine-grained geometry and millimeter-level tolerances required in industrial mechanical design.
AI.method: The paper introduces a million-scale benchmark with 251,000+ fully dimensioned and toleranced 2D orthographic drawings paired with native CAD models, multi-view renderings, mesh, STEP and B-rep representations, and semantic annotations. The benchmark defines four tasks: parametric CAD program synthesis, diagram-to-3D reasoning, annotation-grounded reasoning, and tool-augmented agentic reasoning.
AI.result: Experiments show that current VLMs and CAD-specialized models still struggle with executable program synthesis, fine-grained 3D reconstruction, and reliable enforcement of dimensions and tolerances.
AI.conclusion: The authors will release the benchmark data, evaluation code, and tool interfaces to support future research in industrial-grade CAD generation.

title: Hierarchical Flow Matching for 3D Point Cloud Generation
summary: Generating high-quality 3D point clouds requires capturing both global shape topology and local geometric details. Existing flow-based methods rely on continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) that demand expensive ODE solving and trace estimation during training, while diffusion models require hundreds of iterative denoising steps. Moreover, most approaches adopt single-level generation directly in point space, disregarding the hierarchical structure natural to 3D shapes. We propose Hierarchical Flow Matching (HFM) that extends flow matching to bilevel structure for unconditional 3D point cloud generation. HFM decomposes the task into two levels via optimal-transport flow matching: a \textit{Latent Flow Matching} models the global shape manifold in a compact latent space, and a \textit{Conditional Point Flow Matching} reconstructs detailed point clouds conditioned on the latent code. Both flows are trained with simple MSE regression losses. The resulting straight OT paths enable efficient sampling with as few as 15 Euler steps per flow, while the structured latent space supports downstream tasks including classification. Extensive experiments on ShapeNet and ModelNet benchmarks demonstrate that HFM achieves competitive or even best performance compared with prior state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: HFM extends flow matching to a bilevel (two-level) structure for unconditional 3D point cloud generation, using a latent flow for global shape modeling and a conditional point flow for detail reconstruction, achieving competitive performance with as few as 15 Euler steps per flow.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-based and diffusion-based methods for 3D point cloud generation are computationally expensive (ODE solving, trace estimation, hundreds of denoising steps) and typically generate at a single level, ignoring the hierarchical structure natural to 3D shapes.
AI.method: HFM decomposes point cloud generation into two levels via optimal-transport flow matching: (1) a Latent Flow Matching models the global shape manifold in a compact latent space, and (2) a Conditional Point Flow Matching reconstructs detailed point clouds conditioned on the latent code. Both flows are trained with simple MSE regression losses, and straight OT paths enable efficient sampling.
AI.result: On ShapeNet and ModelNet benchmarks, HFM achieves competitive or even best performance compared with prior state-of-the-art methods, while requiring only as few as 15 Euler steps per flow for efficient sampling. The structured latent space also supports downstream tasks like classification.
AI.conclusion: The bilevel flow matching approach effectively captures both global topology and local geometric details while significantly reducing computational cost compared to CNF-based and diffusion-based alternatives.

title: From Sports to Safety: Benchmarking Proactive Risk Inference in MLLMs
summary: Timely anticipation of physical hazards is essential for real-world safety, yet existing MLLM evaluations focus on harmful content or general risks, leaving proactive physical hazard prediction underexplored. Sports provide a well-suited testbed: accident causes span diverse injury dimensions and pre-accident spatiotemporal cues draw on reasoning capabilities shared with broader safety domains such as autonomous driving and fall detection. We introduce SPRINT (Sports Proactive Risk INference Testbed), a benchmark of 2,888 real-world sports videos (2,440 accident, 448 safe controls) spanning 14 sports and 3 environmental settings. Accident videos feature fine-grained annotations of early hazard cues, accident timing, and hierarchical causes; safe videos are manually verified as accident-free and serve to diagnose prompt-induced false alarms. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs under diverse prompts and temporal windows reveals a sharp gap between hazard sensitivity and understanding: the best model exceeds 95% in signaling hazards yet falls below 50% in identifying their causes. Diagnostic experiments further show that explicit danger queries trigger severe false alarms even on hazard-free videos. These findings indicate that current MLLMs exhibit only superficial proactive safety, lacking stable, cause-grounded early warning, and underscore the need for reliable proactive safety in dynamic physical environments. Data and code will be open-sourced upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: SPRINT is a benchmark of 2,888 real-world sports videos (2,440 accident, 448 safe) with fine-grained hazard annotations, revealing that state-of-the-art MLLMs detect hazards well (>95%) but struggle to identify causes (<50%), and exhibit severe false alarms under explicit danger queries on hazard-free videos, indicating only superficial proactive safety.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM evaluations focus on harmful content or general risks, leaving proactive physical hazard prediction underexplored. Sports provide a suitable testbed for studying physical hazard anticipation and reasoning capabilities shared with broader safety domains.
AI.method: Introduces SPRINT, a benchmark of 2,888 real-world sports videos spanning 14 sports and 3 environmental settings. Accident videos have fine-grained annotations of early hazard cues, accident timing, and hierarchical causes; safe videos are manually verified as accident-free to diagnose prompt-induced false alarms. State-of-the-art MLLMs are evaluated under diverse prompts and temporal windows.
AI.result: The best MLLM exceeds 95% in signaling hazards but falls below 50% in identifying their causes. Explicit danger queries trigger severe false alarms even on hazard-free videos.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs exhibit only superficial proactive safety, lacking stable, cause-grounded early warning, underscoring the need for reliable proactive safety in dynamic physical environments.

title: EffectLearner: World-Aware Object-Effect Reasoning for Real-World Video Object Removal
summary: Video object removal must eliminate not only the target object but also its induced effects while maintaining high-fidelity and spatiotemporally coherent restoration. Existing methods mainly learn object-effect correspondences implicitly from predefined effect categories and fixed data distributions, limiting their generalization to complex real-world scenes involving compositional effects, spatially detached or weakly correlated effects, long-tail physical phenomena, and dynamically evolving interactions. We propose EffectLearner, a semantic-reasoning-enhanced framework that combines a VLM-based Object-Effect Reasoner with a DiT-based Video Eraser. Guided by a structured effect-analysis prompt, the Reasoner performs cross-modal reasoning over a target-highlighted video and extracts compact effect-aware context, which guides the Video Eraser toward comprehensive object-effect removal. Motion-aware mask guidance and motion-consistency supervision further improve removal coverage and spatiotemporal stability under object motion and evolving scene dynamics. To fully exploit the framework in challenging real-world scenarios, we further construct EffectWorld, a paired video dataset specifically designed for complex object-induced effects, and introduce a progressive training curriculum that combines common supervision with complex-effect data. On the standard ROSE-Bench, EffectLearner outperforms existing baselines on most metrics and achieves clear advantages on both EffectWorld-Eval and the challenging EffectWorld-Wild, demonstrating its ability to deliver high-quality video object removal in complex real-world scenes.

AI.tldr: EffectLearner is a video object removal framework combining a VLM-based Object-Effect Reasoner with a DiT-based Video Eraser, enhanced by a new EffectWorld dataset and progressive training curriculum to handle complex object-induced effects in real-world scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing video object removal methods learn object-effect correspondences implicitly from predefined effect categories and fixed data distributions, which limits generalization to complex real-world scenes involving compositional effects, detached/weakly correlated effects, long-tail phenomena, and dynamically evolving interactions.
AI.method: EffectLearner combines (1) a VLM-based Object-Effect Reasoner that performs cross-modal reasoning over target-highlighted videos using a structured effect-analysis prompt to extract effect-aware context, and (2) a DiT-based Video Eraser guided by this context. Motion-aware mask guidance and motion-consistency supervision improve removal coverage and spatiotemporal stability. A new paired dataset EffectWorld is constructed and a progressive training curriculum combines common supervision with complex-effect data.
AI.result: On ROSE-Bench, EffectLearner outperforms existing baselines on most metrics, and achieves clear advantages on both EffectWorld-Eval and the challenging EffectWorld-Wild, demonstrating high-quality video object removal in complex real-world scenes.
AI.conclusion: Semantic reasoning about object-effect relationships, combined with tailored data and training strategies, enables robust video object removal that handles compositional, weakly correlated, long-tail, and dynamic effects in real-world scenarios.

title: CoordRefer: Coordinate-Aware 3D Visual Grounding from Multiview Images
summary: Multiview image-based 3D visual grounding predicts a coordinate frame to define a coordinate system and then regresses a 3D bounding box for localization. However, existing methods jointly optimize coordinate frame selection and box regression, leading to coordinate-relative box ambiguity and degraded grounding performance. This ambiguity arises because the same box admits different numerical representations across coordinate frames, creating multiple optimization targets and yielding invalid compromise predictions. To tackle this challenge, we propose CoordRefer, a coordinate-aware framework that decouples coordinate frame selection from coordinate-conditioned grounding. CoordRefer first selects a reference frame to define the coordinate system and then conditions 3D box prediction on the coordinate system. We perform coordinate-aware supervised fine-tuning to establish coordinate frame selection and coordinate-conditioned box regression, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization with 3D IoU-based rewards to align both stages with downstream grounding quality. On ScanRefer with Qwen3-VL-2B, CoordRefer achieves gains of 11% in Acc@0.25 and 7% in Acc@0.5 over the coordinate-agnostic baseline, while its geometrically refined variant surpasses methods using explicit 3D inputs.

AI.tldr: CoordRefer is a coordinate-aware framework for multiview image-based 3D visual grounding that decouples coordinate frame selection from coordinate-conditioned box regression, using coordinate-aware supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization with 3D IoU-based rewards to resolve coordinate-relative box ambiguity and improve grounding performance.
AI.motivation: Existing multiview image-based 3D visual grounding methods jointly optimize coordinate frame selection and box regression, which creates coordinate-relative box ambiguity. Since the same 3D box can have different numerical representations across different coordinate frames, this leads to multiple conflicting optimization targets and produces invalid compromise predictions that degrade grounding performance.
AI.method: CoordRefer decouples the two-stage process: (1) it first selects a reference frame to define the coordinate system, then (2) conditions 3D box prediction on that chosen coordinate system. The framework employs coordinate-aware supervised fine-tuning to establish both coordinate frame selection and coordinate-conditioned box regression, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization with 3D IoU-based rewards to align both stages with downstream grounding quality.
AI.result: On ScanRefer with Qwen3-VL-2B, CoordRefer achieves gains of 11% in Acc@0.25 and 7% in Acc@0.5 over the coordinate-agnostic baseline. Its geometrically refined variant surpasses methods that use explicit 3D inputs.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling coordinate frame selection from coordinate-conditioned grounding resolves the coordinate-relative box ambiguity problem, leading to significantly improved 3D visual grounding performance. The proposed coordination-aware training strategy with reinforcement learning alignment is effective, even enabling the approach to outperform methods that rely on explicit 3D data.

title: Beyond Frame Selection: Rethinking Long-Video Understanding with MLLMs
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong progress in video understanding, yet it remains challenging because the token limitation makes MLLMs difficult to capture temporally sparse evidence. Existing methods typically rely on uniform sampling, or frame selection, but these strategies usually optimize either broad temporal coverage or local relevance, making it difficult to preserve both global storyline context and fine-grained evidence. We propose VideoRouter(VR) that rethinks long-video understanding as coordinating complementary evidence views rather than selecting a single subset of frames. It first organizes each video into a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy, which partition the video into coarse-to-fine temporally coherent segments. In this hierarchy, upper-level nodes capture broad storyline context and event progression, while lower-level nodes preserve fine-grained local details and evidence-bearing moments. This naturally gives rise to two complementary views: a global view for coverage-oriented reasoning and a local view for detail-oriented evidence recovery. We further introduce a verification-guided router to determine which view is better supported by the selected evidence and select the final answer. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed design through extensive experiments, showing that the verification-guided router effectively coordinates global and local reasoning, and that, on VideoMME, our method outperforms state-of-the-art frame selection methods by 2.9 points, respectively, under the LLaVA-Video-7B backbone. We will release the code.

AI.tldr: VideoRouter (VR) rethinks long-video understanding by coordinating complementary evidence views—a global view for broad storyline coverage and a local view for fine-grained detail recovery—rather than selecting a single subset of frames. It builds a question-agnostic temporal hierarchy that partitions video into coarse-to-fine temporally coherent segments, then uses a verification-guided router to select the best-supported answer, outperforming state-of-the-art frame selection methods by 2.9 points on VideoMME with LLaVA-Video-7B.
