Such de-identification protects the metadata but not the pixels, and---apart from scans that directly contain facial structures---whether the image content itself identifies the patient has received little scrutiny. We investigate this question by learning a cycle-consistent correspondence between a cross-sectional medical image and a non-medical, patient-identifying image, using a pair of coupled, cycle-consistent variational autoencoders. From a held-out scan, the model recovers a recognisable likeness of the patient (identity-region MAE = 0.163); conversely, it synthesises a scan from such an image. These results indicate that a de-identified medical scan remains identifying---it is, in effect, a photograph of the patient---and that imaging data should be governed as biometric data rather than as anonymisable records. To support reproducibility, the code and trained models are shared at https://github.com/attilasimko/public-repository.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that de-identified medical images (with metadata removed) still contain pixel-level information that can identify patients. Using coupled, cycle-consistent variational autoencoders, the authors learn a correspondence between cross-sectional medical scans and patient-identifying photographs, successfully recovering recognizable likenesses from held-out scans and synthesizing scans from photos. They conclude that medical imaging data should be treated as biometric data, not anonymizable records.
AI.motivation: Current de-identification practices for medical images only remove metadata (names, dates), leaving pixel content intact. The question of whether image content itself can identify a patient has received little scrutiny, especially for scans not directly containing facial structures. This paper investigates whether such de-identified scans remain identifying.
AI.method: The authors learn a cycle-consistent correspondence between cross-sectional medical images and non-medical, patient-identifying images (photographs) using a pair of coupled, cycle-consistent variational autoencoders. The model maps between the two image domains to recover identity information.
AI.result: From a held-out scan, the model recovers a recognisable likeness of the patient (identity-region MAE = 0.163). Conversely, it can synthesise a medical scan from a patient-identifying image. These results demonstrate that de-identified medical scans retain patient-identifying information in the pixels themselves.
AI.conclusion: De-identified medical scans are effectively photographs of the patient and remain identifying. Medical imaging data should therefore be governed as biometric data rather than as anonymisable records. Code and trained models are released for reproducibility.

title: Respect Your Zero-Shot Uncertainty: Conservative Calibration for Test-Time-Adapted Vision-Language Models
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) can improve the recognition accuracy of vision-language models under distribution shift, but often degrades calibration, making predictive confidence unreliable for downstream decision-making. Many existing label-free calibration approaches are either coupled to prompt optimization or rely on logit-range statistics that provide only a coarse characterization of the predictive distribution. We show that TTA can increase confidence and reduce entropy even when the top-1 prediction and its correctness remain unchanged, a failure mode we term prediction-preserving sharpening. Across diverse TTA methods and benchmarks, larger entropy reductions relative to paired zero-shot predictions are associated with greater increases in Expected Calibration Error (ECE). On entropy-reduced samples, confidence gains also tend to exceed accuracy gains. Based on these findings, we propose Zero-Shot-Anchored Entropy Calibration (ZAEC), a label-free post-hoc method that uses zero-shot entropy as a sample-specific uncertainty reference. ZAEC selectively restores the zero-shot entropy of sharpened predictions through minimal temperature scaling while leaving all other predictions unchanged. It requires no labeled calibration data or learned parameters and preserves class rankings and classification accuracy. Across five TTA methods and 15 datasets, ZAEC achieves the lowest post-hoc macro-average ECE on ViT-B/16, with consistent gains on RN50.

AI.tldr: ZAEC is a label-free post-hoc calibration method that uses zero-shot entropy as a sample-specific uncertainty reference to restore calibration for test-time adapted vision-language models, achieving the lowest macro-average ECE across five TTA methods and 15 datasets.
AI.motivation: Test-time adaptation (TTA) improves recognition accuracy of vision-language models under distribution shift but degrades calibration, making predictive confidence unreliable for downstream decision-making. Existing label-free calibration approaches are either coupled to prompt optimization or rely on coarse logit-range statistics. The authors identify a failure mode called prediction-preserving sharpening, where TTA increases confidence and reduces entropy even when the top-1 prediction and correctness remain unchanged, leading to miscalibration.
AI.method: The paper first analyzes TTA's calibration degradation, showing that larger entropy reductions relative to paired zero-shot predictions correlate with greater increases in Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Based on these findings, they propose Zero-Shot-Anchored Entropy Calibration (ZAEC), a post-hoc method that uses zero-shot entropy as a sample-specific uncertainty reference. ZAEC restores zero-shot entropy for sharpened predictions via minimal temperature scaling while leaving other predictions unchanged. It requires no labeled calibration data or learned parameters.
AI.result: Across five TTA methods and 15 datasets, ZAEC achieves the lowest post-hoc macro-average ECE on ViT-B/16 with consistent gains on RN50. It preserves class rankings and classification accuracy while requiring no calibration data or learned parameters.
AI.conclusion: ZAEC demonstrates that zero-shot entropies serve as effective sample-specific uncertainty references for calibrating test-time adapted models, offering a simple, parameter-free, and label-free solution to the calibration degradation introduced by TTA.

title: Big, Bright, or Invisible: A Frozen-Feature Benchmark of 3D CT Foundation Models
summary: Routine CT interpretation is inherently comprehensive, capturing incidental findings across the entire scan volume. 3D CT foundation models could assist this process by providing generalizable representations of anatomy and pathology. To evaluate their diagnostic breadth, we benchmark ten frozen CT encoders across three cohorts of thoracic CT scans, including an unseen internal clinical dataset, using $k$-nearest neighbors, zero-shot prompting, and linear probing. We find no universal state-of-the-art, with rankings fluctuating significantly depending on the evaluation context. While models combining fine-grained image tokenization with vision-language alignment generally perform best, a lightweight supervised encoder remains highly competitive, demonstrating that explicit labels can effectively substitute for scale. Crucially, rather than model architecture, we observe that the primary determinant of performance is a physical bottleneck: a finding's detectability scales with its contrast against surrounding tissue and its spatial extent. Through controlled within-organ comparisons, we empirically demonstrate that widespread or high-contrast abnormalities, such as devices and effusions, are reliably recovered. Conversely, small, low-contrast focal lesions remain a persistent challenge across all evaluated encoders. We attribute this to the inherent limitations of globally pooled embeddings, suggesting that accurately representing small, low-contrast structures will require region- or lesion-level pretraining.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks ten frozen 3D CT foundation model encoders across three thoracic CT datasets to evaluate their diagnostic breadth, finding that no single model is universally superior, and that performance is primarily governed by a physical bottleneck—lesion detectability scales with contrast and spatial extent—rather than model architecture. Small, low-contrast lesions remain poorly represented due to global pooling limitations.
AI.motivation: Routine CT interpretation requires comprehensive detection of incidental findings across the entire scan volume. 3D CT foundation models could potentially assist this process, but their diagnostic breadth—how well they represent diverse anatomy and pathology—has not been systematically evaluated. The authors aim to benchmark these models to understand their actual capabilities and limitations in a clinically meaningful context.
AI.method: The authors benchmark ten frozen CT encoders across three thoracic CT cohorts (including an unseen internal clinical dataset) using three evaluation protocols: k-nearest neighbors, zero-shot prompting, and linear probing. They systematically compare model rankings across evaluation contexts and analyze performance as a function of finding characteristics (contrast and spatial extent) through controlled within-organ comparisons.
AI.result: No universal state-of-the-art model exists; rankings fluctuate significantly by evaluation context. Models combining fine-grained image tokenization with vision-language alignment generally perform best, but a lightweight supervised encoder remains highly competitive, showing labels can substitute for scale. The primary performance determinant is not model architecture but a physical bottleneck: detectability scales with contrast and spatial extent. Widespread/high-contrast abnormalities (devices, effusions) are reliably recovered, while small, low-contrast focal lesions remain challenging across all encoders.
AI.conclusion: Globally pooled embeddings have inherent limitations for representing small, low-contrast structures. Future progress in 3D CT foundation models for comprehensive diagnostic support will likely require region- or lesion-level pretraining strategies rather than relying solely on architecture improvements or model scale.

title: Topology-Aware Neighborhood Learning for Source-Free Cross-Scene Hyperspectral Image Classification
summary: Domain adaptation has advanced cross-scene hyperspectral image classification, significantly improving discriminative capability in complex scenarios. However, privacy rules or storage limits often block access to data from the source domain. Conventional domain adaptation methods become impractical, severely restricting their utility in realistic remote sensing scenarios. To tackle this challenge, we propose a topology-aware source-free learning framework. We first introduce the entropy momentum pseudo-labeling (EMP) to refine k-means assignments by leveraging entropy-aware confidence and temporal prediction momentum. Under the guidance of the refined pseudo-labels, we further utilize the contextual neighborhood topology (CNT) to exploit the intrinsic geometric structure of the target feature space. Combining the global structural information extracted by collaborative representation with the local similarity information modeled by nearest neighbor search, the CNT accomplishes the comprehensive encoding of manifold-level geometric properties in the target domain feature space. The overall objective integrates cross-entropy on refined pseudo-labels, log inner product-based topology consistency, and an information-maximization term for balanced classification, ensuring stable adaptation in the source-free setting. Extensive experiments on three typical cross-scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method exceeds state-of-the-art performance, and ablation studies further validate the contribution of each module. The results highlight the critical role of topology-aware modeling in achieving robust and accurate classification without source data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a topology-aware source-free learning framework for cross-scene hyperspectral image classification, addressing the challenge when source domain data is inaccessible due to privacy or storage constraints. The method combines entropy momentum pseudo-labeling (EMP) for refining k-means assignments and contextual neighborhood topology (CNT) for exploiting geometric structure in the target feature space, achieving state-of-the-art performance on three cross-scenario benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Conventional domain adaptation methods fail when source domain data is unavailable due to privacy rules or storage limits, which commonly occurs in realistic remote sensing scenarios. This severely restricts the practical utility of existing adaptation approaches, motivating the need for source-free domain adaptation in hyperspectral image classification.
AI.method: The framework introduces two key components: (1) Entropy momentum pseudo-labeling (EMP) that refines k-means assignments using entropy-aware confidence and temporal prediction momentum; and (2) Contextual neighborhood topology (CNT) that encodes manifold-level geometric properties by combining global structural information from collaborative representation with local similarity from nearest neighbor search. The overall loss integrates cross-entropy on refined pseudo-labels, log inner product-based topology consistency, and an information-maximization term for balanced classification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three typical cross-scenario benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method exceeds state-of-the-art performance. Ablation studies validate the contribution of each module, highlighting the critical role of topology-aware modeling for robust and accurate classification without source data.
AI.conclusion: The results confirm that topology-aware modeling is essential for achieving robust and accurate source-free domain adaptation in hyperspectral image classification, providing a practical solution for realistic remote sensing scenarios where source data access is restricted.

title: Diff-VF: Training-free High-quality Long Video Generation via Diffusion Model
comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications (TOMM)
summary: Recently, diffusion models have made great progress in video generation. However, most existing video diffusion models are trained with short videos, and degrade when extrapolated to long videos, struggling to maintain long-range temporal coherence while retaining diverse motions. To generate consistent, high-quality and dynamic long videos, we propose Diff-VF, a training-free, plug-and-play and model-agnostic framework that converts existing short-video diffusion backbones into long-video generators without modifying or fine-tuning the base model. Diff-VF couples three complementary strategies: Hybrid Noise Initialization (HNI) to constrain global semantics, Weighted Window Sampling (WWS) to remove inter-window discontinuities, and Temporal Extended Sampling (TES) to establish long-range dependencies with a timestep-varying fusion. We further extend Diff-VF to long-video enhancement via Skip Residual Guidance that balances fidelity and realism through timestep-dependent guidance. VBench-Long evaluation results show that Diff-VF achieves a more favorable balance between temporal coherence and motion diversity than base models and recent training-free long video generation baselines, including FreeNoise, FreeLong, and RIFLEx, while maintaining competitive frame-wise quality. Experiments on two base models demonstrate the applicability to video diffusion models with different spatial-temporal modeling strategies. Extensive ablations validate the contribution of each component and hyperparameters.

AI.tldr: Diff-VF is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that converts existing short-video diffusion models into long-video generators by coupling three strategies: Hybrid Noise Initialization (HNI), Weighted Window Sampling (WWS), and Temporal Extended Sampling (TES), plus Skip Residual Guidance for long-video enhancement.
AI.motivation: Most existing video diffusion models are trained on short videos and degrade when extrapolated to long videos, struggling to maintain long-range temporal coherence while retaining diverse motions.
AI.method: Diff-VF is a model-agnostic, training-free framework that combines: (1) Hybrid Noise Initialization (HNI) to constrain global semantics, (2) Weighted Window Sampling (WWS) to remove inter-window discontinuities, (3) Temporal Extended Sampling (TES) to establish long-range dependencies with timestep-varying fusion, and Skip Residual Guidance (SRG) for long-video enhancement that balances fidelity and realism.
AI.result: On VBench-Long, Diff-VF achieves a more favorable balance between temporal coherence and motion diversity than base models and recent training-free baselines (FreeNoise, FreeLong, RIFLEx), while maintaining competitive frame-wise quality. Experiments on two base models demonstrate applicability across different spatial-temporal modeling strategies.
AI.conclusion: Diff-VF effectively converts short-video diffusion backbones into long-video generators without modification or fine-tuning, achieving better temporal coherence vs. motion diversity trade-offs. Extensive ablations validate the contribution of each component and hyperparameters.

title: Multi-Year Geospatial Reasoning using Interannually-Consistent Historical Predictions as a Free Input Modality
summary: Machine learning, and deep networks in particular, are increasingly used to derive higher-level Earth observation (EO) products such as annual land-cover and crop-type maps. Many are generated operationally: each year a new acquisition is processed, typically with the same model, extending a multi-year archive. In the process these systems accumulate two kinds of useful signal that are almost never fed back into the model: the system's own archive of past predictions, and ancillary layers produced by other partners in a processing consortium. Both are normally used outside the network, as rule-based post-processing or a fixed input mask. Using the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service High Resolution Layer (HRL) Croplands crop-type product as a testbed, we show that bringing both signals inside the model turns a single-year, single-task pixel classifier into one that reasons across years. We introduce a Crop Type (CTY) embedding encoder that represents each past prediction as a confidence-scaled, time-ordered categorical token and attends over the year axis, and we study how the externally provided Base Vegetation Layer (BVL) mask should be represented in the model's inputs and outputs. To compare designs fairly when they relabel non-crop pixels, we evaluate on the 18 crop classes only and report precision and recall separately. On a pan-European dataset of about 5.4M labelled pixels, adding the prediction history raises crop-only F1 by 1.6 percentage points (pp) and, more importantly, corrects a recall-skewed error profile, with the largest gains on perennial and tree crops (olives +4.6, fruits +3.7, nuts +3.2 pp). Representing the BVL mask consistently in both the history and the target year adds about 2.5 pp on the crop classes. The approach is a low-cost recipe for any recurring geospatial or foundation model that emits class maps.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes incorporating past prediction archives and ancillary layers (like the BVL mask) into deep learning models for crop-type classification from Earth observation data, rather than using them as external post-processing. The method introduces a Crop Type (CTY) embedding encoder that represents each past prediction as a confidence-scaled, time-ordered categorical token attending over the year axis. On 5.4M pan-European labelled pixels, adding prediction history improves crop-only F1 by 1.6 pp and corrects recall-skewed error profiles, with largest gains on perennial crops. The approach offers a low-cost recipe for any recurring geospatial model emitting class maps.
AI.motivation: Operational Earth observation systems accumulate two valuable signals—past prediction archives and ancillary layers from partner consortia—but these are almost never fed back into the model, being used instead as external post-processing or fixed input masks. The paper aims to bring these signals inside the model to enable reasoning across years.
AI.method: The paper introduces a Crop Type (CTY) embedding encoder that represents each past prediction as a confidence-scaled, time-ordered categorical token and attends over the year axis. It also studies how the externally provided Base Vegetation Layer (BVL) mask should be represented in the model's inputs and outputs, comparing designs under a fair evaluation protocol that relabels non-crop pixels and reports precision/recall separately on 18 crop classes.
AI.result: On a pan-European dataset of ~5.4M labelled pixels, adding prediction history raises crop-only F1 by 1.6 percentage points and corrects a recall-skewed error profile, with the largest gains on perennial and tree crops (olives +4.6, fruits +3.7, nuts +3.2 pp). Representing the BVL mask consistently in both history and target year adds ~2.5 pp on crop classes.
AI.conclusion: The approach transforms a single-year, single-task pixel classifier into one that reasons across years by incorporating historical predictions and ancillary layers into the model itself. It is a low-cost, broadly applicable recipe for any recurring geospatial or foundation model that emits class maps.

title: Universal Concept Disruption for SAM3 Image Segmentation
summary: SAM3 extends promptable segmentation from geometry-driven mask prediction to open-vocabulary concept segmentation, where a text-conditioned grounding model decides whether a concept is present and segments all matching instances. While this presence-gated design improves concept-level prediction, its adversarial robustness remains unexplored. In this paper, we introduce Universal Concept Disruption (UCD), the first universal cross-concept adversarial attack tailored to SAM3 image segmentation. UCD learns a single bounded image perturbation from (image, noun-phrase) pairs and attacks SAM3 as an integrated concept-grounding system. It jointly disrupts the text-conditioned input path, maximizes divergence in prompt-shared visual features, suppresses the final presence-gated concept scores, and corrupts the spatial validity of retained masks through area collapse and clean-mask Dice disruption. Across SACo-Gold, LVIS, RefCOCO, PhraseCut, and OpenImages datasets, UCD consistently outperforms all baselines under a matched evaluation protocol, reducing average mask AP from 59.43 to 18.73 and average cgF1 from 50.32 to 20.49. The learned perturbation also transfers to SAM3.1 and to SAM3 video inference without re-optimization, while prompt ensembling, lightweight head fine-tuning, and temporal filtering provide limited recovery.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Universal Concept Disruption (UCD), the first universal cross-concept adversarial attack targeting SAM3's open-vocabulary concept segmentation system. UCD learns a single bounded perturbation that jointly disrupts multiple components of SAM3, reducing average mask AP from 59.43 to 18.73 and cgF1 from 50.32 to 20.49 across five datasets, while transferring to SAM3.1 and SAM3 video inference without re-optimization.
AI.motivation: While SAM3 extends promptable segmentation to open-vocabulary concept segmentation with a presence-gated design, its adversarial robustness has not been explored. This gap is significant because the integrated concept-grounding architecture may be vulnerable to attacks that existing segmentation attack methods fail to exploit.
AI.method: UCD learns a single bounded image perturbation from (image, noun-phrase) pairs and attacks SAM3 as an integrated concept-grounding system. It jointly: (1) disrupts the text-conditioned input path, (2) maximizes divergence in prompt-shared visual features, (3) suppresses final presence-gated concept scores, and (4) corrupts spatial validity of retained masks through area collapse and clean-mask Dice disruption.
AI.result: Across SACo-Gold, LVIS, RefCOCO, PhraseCut, and OpenImages, UCD consistently outperforms all baselines under matched evaluation, reducing average mask AP from 59.43 to 18.73 and average cgF1 from 50.32 to 20.49. The perturbation transfers to SAM3.1 and SAM3 video inference without re-optimization. Defenses (prompt ensembling, head fine-tuning, temporal filtering) provide only limited recovery.
AI.conclusion: The presence-gated design of SAM3 is vulnerable to universal cross-concept adversarial attacks, and existing defenses offer insufficient protection against such attacks.

title: Wan-Animate-2: Pushing the Application Boundaries of Character Animation
summary: Character image animation remains a foundational yet challenging task in computer vision. Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into three paradigms: methods based on explicit motion representations suffer from extraction errors and identity drift; methods based on implicit motion features lose fine-grained dynamics through compression; and in-context learning approaches avoid intermediate representations but incur prohibitive computational costs. Furthermore, all current systems are designed for offline synthesis, unable to meet the real-time requirements of interactive applications such as digital avatars and live-streaming hosts. To address these limitations, we present Wan-Animate-2, an end-to-end character animation framework that directly consumes the driving video within a redesigned Diffusion Transformer. Our architecture achieves superior motion fidelity and identity preservation by eliminating intermediate motion extractors entirely. We further introduce text driven viewpoint control that decouples the output camera perspective from the driving video--a capability rarely supported by prior character animation methods that rely on explicit motion representations. Beyond generation quality, we present Wan-Animate-2-Lite, an efficient variant that reduces inference latency to real-time thresholds through a three-stage training paradigm: teacher forcing pretraining with error buffer mechanism, and Self-Forcing distillation with chunk-wise backpropagation. This enables streaming character animation for interactive applications, opening new deployment scenarios that were previously infeasible. Qualitative evaluations and user studies demonstrate that Wan-Animate-2 achieves high-fidelity animation results across diverse characters and motion patterns. To foster further research and community development, we will release the Wan-Animate-2-Base model weights to the public.

AI.tldr: Wan-Animate-2 is an end-to-end character animation framework using a redesigned Diffusion Transformer that directly consumes driving videos without intermediate motion extractors, achieving superior motion fidelity and identity preservation. It also introduces text-driven viewpoint control and a Lite variant with real-time inference latency for streaming interactive applications.
AI.motivation: Existing character animation methods fall into three paradigms (explicit motion representations, implicit motion features, in-context learning), each with limitations including extraction errors, identity drift, loss of fine-grained dynamics, or prohibitive computational costs. Additionally, all current systems are offline-only and cannot meet real-time requirements for interactive applications like digital avatars and live-streaming hosts.
AI.method: An end-to-end Diffusion Transformer architecture that directly consumes driving video without intermediate motion extractors, eliminating the need for explicit motion representations. It introduces text-driven viewpoint control decoupled from the driving video. The Lite variant achieves real-time inference through a three-stage training paradigm: teacher forcing pretraining with error buffer mechanism, and Self-Forcing distillation with chunk-wise backpropagation.
AI.result: Qualitative evaluations and user studies demonstrate high-fidelity animation results across diverse characters and motion patterns. The Lite variant reduces inference latency to real-time thresholds, enabling streaming character animation for interactive applications.
AI.conclusion: Wan-Animate-2 addresses the limitations of prior character animation paradigms by providing an end-to-end framework with superior quality, viewpoint control, and real-time capability for interactive deployment scenarios. The authors will release the Wan-Animate-2-Base model weights to foster further research.

title: Iterate or Widen? When Test-Time Refinement Helps LiDAR Scene Completion: A Controlled Study of Evidence Geometry, Training Coverage, and Compute
summary: Should a completion model spend extra test-time compute by iterating, or spend a similar parameter budget on a wider one-shot predictor? The answer is easily confounded by denoising curricula, corruption augmentation, capacity, and unpaired evaluation. We study this question in LiDAR semantic scene completion by comparing a one-shot predictor, a parameter-matched wider predictor, and a weight-tied multigrid refiner initialized from the same frozen predictor. The protocol separates coherent region removal, independent thinning, range-dependent attenuation, and additive clutter while preserving exact scene-condition pairing. Across five training seeds and 815 SemanticKITTI sequence-08 frames, the full iterative system improves mIoU over the wide control by 0.911 points under contiguous angular removal, with a 95% moving-block bootstrap interval of [0.804, 1.040] that clears a predeclared 0.5-point practical margin. Under independent 75% thinning, iteration adds only 0.300 points [0.166, 0.436], whereas observation-family augmentation adds 5.975 points [5.662, 6.140]. Neither intervention repairs additive clutter. The iterative system also costs 10.74 ms and 0.75 GiB per frame, versus 6.25 ms and 0.23 GiB for the wide control. These results establish a geometry-conditioned empirical boundary rather than a universal advantage: coherent gaps can justify fixed-depth refinement, broadly thinned evidence is addressed more effectively by training coverage, and spurious evidence requires a different robustness mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether iterative test-time computation in a completion model outperforms a parameter-matched one-shot predictor for LiDAR semantic scene completion. Using a carefully controlled protocol separating different types of corruption (coherent removal, thinning, attenuation, clutter), the authors find that iterative refinement provides meaningful gains (0.911 mIoU) for contiguous angular removal, but training-time augmentation is far more effective for independent thinning (5.975 mIoU), and neither helps with additive clutter. The iterative system also incurs higher computational costs (10.74 ms vs 6.25 ms, 0.75 GiB vs 0.23 GiB).
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a fundamental and practically important question: should a completion model spend extra compute at test time through iterative refinement, or is it better to allocate that budget toward a wider one-shot model? This question is often obscured by confounds such as denoising curricula, corruption augmentation, capacity mismatches, and unpaired evaluation. The authors aim to establish a clean, geometry-conditioned empirical boundary rather than a universal claim about iterative vs. wider models.
AI.method: The study compares three models: (1) a one-shot predictor, (2) a parameter-matched wider predictor, and (3) a weight-tied multigrid refiner initialized from the same frozen predictor. The experimental protocol systematically separates four corruption types—coherent region removal, independent thinning, range-dependent attenuation, and additive clutter—while preserving exact scene-condition pairing. Experiments use five training seeds across 815 SemanticKITTI sequence-08 frames, with 95% moving-block bootstrap confidence intervals and a predeclared 0.5-point practical margin for statistical comparison.
AI.result: The full iterative system improves mIoU over the wide control by 0.911 points for contiguous angular removal (bootstrap CI [0.804, 1.040], clearing the 0.5-point margin). Under independent 75% thinning, iteration adds only 0.300 points (CI [0.166, 0.436]), while observation-family augmentation adds 5.975 points (CI [5.662, 6.140]). Neither intervention repairs additive clutter. The iterative system costs 10.74 ms and 0.75 GiB per frame versus 6.25 ms and 0.23 GiB for the wide control.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a geometry-conditioned empirical boundary: iterative refinement is justified for coherent gaps (fixed-depth refinement helps with contiguous missing regions), but broad thinning is better addressed by training coverage (augmentation), and spurious evidence requires a fundamentally different robustness mechanism. There is no universal advantage of iteration over a wider one-shot predictor—the right choice depends on the nature of the corruption and the compute/capacity trade-off.

title: PaCoNet: Deep Data Extraction for Parallel Coordinates
summary: Extracting data from visualizations has long challenged computer vision, with current research focused on bar, line, and pie charts, among other low-dimensional visualizations. However, parallel coordinates as a widely used high-dimensional data visualization approach, remain largely unexplored in this context. As parallel coordinate plots can quickly become cluttered and difficult to interpret when poorly designed or densely populated, automated data extraction from such visualizations is of particular interest. In this paper, we propose PaCoNet, the first approach for parallel coordinate data extraction. PaCoNet not only extracts line coordinates, but also enables the extraction of individual data samples for further analysis. Towards this end, we make the following contributions. We present the first deep learning approach tailored for parallel coordinate analysis, and demonstrate that it outperforms unadapted baselines by a significant margin. We further introduce a large-scale parallel coordinate dataset for training and testing. Together, these key contributions enable for the first time the automated analysis and redesign of parallel coordinate plots. PaCoNet thus lays the groundwork for complex visualization analysis, and further advances the intersection of computer vision and data visualization. All code, trained models, and data generation scripts will be made publicly available upon acceptance of the paper.

AI.tldr: PaCoNet is the first deep learning approach for automated data extraction from parallel coordinate plots, outperforming unadapted baselines significantly and introducing a large-scale dataset. It enables extraction of both line coordinates and individual data samples, laying groundwork for automated analysis and redesign of parallel coordinate visualizations.
AI.motivation: While computer vision research has addressed data extraction from bar, line, and pie charts, parallel coordinates—a widely used high-dimensional visualization technique—remain unexplored. Since parallel coordinate plots can become cluttered and difficult to interpret, automated data extraction from such visualizations is of particular interest and need.
AI.method: PaCoNet is a novel deep learning approach specifically tailored for parallel coordinate analysis. It extracts line coordinates and individual data samples from parallel coordinate plots. The authors also create and release a large-scale parallel coordinate dataset for training and testing purposes.
AI.result: PaCoNet significantly outperforms unadapted baseline methods for parallel coordinate data extraction. The approach enables, for the first time, automated analysis and redesign of parallel coordinate plots.
AI.conclusion: PaCoNet lays the groundwork for complex visualization analysis, advancing the intersection of computer vision and data visualization. All code, trained models, and data generation scripts will be released publicly.

title: DARAD: Dual Adapters and Ranking-Aware Distillation for Continual Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval
summary: With the rapid growth of Earth observation technologies, remote sensing archives are rapidly expanding, making remote sensing image-text retrieval (RS-ITR) increasingly important. However, continual RS-ITR remains challenging because scale variation and distribution shifts in RS aggravate cross-modal alignment space distortion, making it difficult for existing continual learning (CL) methods to support reliable continual retrieval. To address this challenge, we propose DARAD, a dual-adapter and ranking-aware distillation framework that preserves the historical cross-modal ranking structure while learning new visual and textual concepts from evolving archives. Specifically, the visual branch introduces a spatial fusion adapter, which integrates coarse regional cues and fine-grained patch cues to accommodate RS scale variation while anchoring visual updates to the pretrained alignment space. The textual branch employs multi-expert semantic routing, which separates shared textual semantics from semantically specialized residuals to absorb newly emerging descriptions while constraining global text embedding drift. Furthermore, bidirectional ranking distillation uses a frozen teacher model and historical anchors to preserve the historical cross-modal ranking structure, thereby mitigating alignment space distortion across continual stages. Experiments under a multi-stage continual retrieval protocol show that DARAD achieves superior performance over existing CL methods, improving adaptation to newly arrived data while maintaining effectiveness on historical data.

AI.tldr: DARAD is a dual-adapter and ranking-aware distillation framework for continual remote sensing image-text retrieval, addressing scale variation and distribution shifts that distort cross-modal alignment space.
AI.motivation: Remote sensing archives are rapidly expanding, but continual RS-ITR is challenging because scale variation and distribution shifts in RS distort cross-modal alignment space, making existing continual learning methods unreliable for continual retrieval.
AI.method: DARAD has three key components: (1) a spatial fusion adapter in the visual branch that integrates coarse regional and fine-grained patch cues to handle scale variation while anchoring to pretrained alignment space; (2) multi-expert semantic routing in the textual branch that separates shared semantics from specialized residuals to absorb new descriptions while constraining text embedding drift; and (3) bidirectional ranking distillation using a frozen teacher model and historical anchors to preserve historical cross-modal ranking structure.
AI.result: Under a multi-stage continual retrieval protocol, DARAD achieves superior performance over existing CL methods, improving adaptation to newly arrived data while maintaining effectiveness on historical data.
AI.conclusion: DARAD effectively mitigates alignment space distortion in continual RS-ITR by preserving historical ranking structure while adapting to new visual and textual concepts, outperforming existing continual learning methods.

title: Learning from Failures: Retrieval-Centric CoT via Hard Negatives for Unified Multimodal Retrieval
summary: Unified multimodal retrieval aims to identify candidates that satisfy complex user intent expressed through heterogeneous inputs. Although Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM)-based retrievers are efficient and scalable, directly encoding raw multimodal inputs often misses fine-grained discriminative cues, leading to confusion among semantically similar candidates. Recent methods mitigate this limitation by generating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) rationales to enrich the query representation. However, such reasoning is typically derived from the query alone: it explains what the query describes, but not what the retriever misunderstands. We argue that effective retrieval reasoning should instead be conditioned on retrieval feedback. Based on this insight, we introduce UniME-R1, an embedder-adviser framework that learns to reason over initially retrieved candidates and generate Retrieval-Centric Chain-of-Thought (RC-CoT). The adviser analyzes candidates individually to identify the discriminative cues confused by the embedder. If the target appears in the initial top-k set, UniME-R1 directly reranks the candidates; otherwise, it generates RC-CoT to refine the retrieval direction and performs full-corpus re-retrieval with a dual-mode embedder. To train the framework, we mine hard negatives to simulate realistic retrieval failures, jointly optimize direct retrieval and RC-CoT-augmented retrieval, and align the adviser with retrieval outcomes through supervised learning and retrieval-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and a diverse set of general multimodal retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that UniME-R1 consistently improves retrieval performance over strong baselines.

AI.tldr: UniME-R1 is an embedder-adviser framework for unified multimodal retrieval that improves LVLM-based retrievers by generating Retrieval-Centric Chain-of-Thought (RC-CoT) reasoning conditioned on retrieval feedback, not just the query alone. The adviser analyzes initial retrieved candidates to identify discriminative cues the embedder confuses, and either reranks candidates directly or generates RC-CoT to refine the retrieval direction and re-retrieve the full corpus. Trained with hard-negative mining, joint optimization of direct and RC-CoT-augmented retrieval, and retrieval-oriented RL, it consistently outperforms strong baselines on MMEB-V2 and general multimodal benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LVLM-based multimodal retrievers miss fine-grained discriminative cues when encoding raw inputs, leading to confusion among semantically similar candidates. Prior CoT augmentation methods generate reasoning from the query alone, which explains what the query describes but not what the retriever misunderstands. The authors argue that effective retrieval reasoning should be conditioned on retrieval feedback.
AI.method: UniME-R1 introduces an embedder-adviser framework with three key components: (1) The adviser analyzes initially retrieved candidates to identify discriminative cues confused by the embedder and generates Retrieval-Centric Chain-of-Thought (RC-CoT); (2) A dual-mode strategy where candidates in the top-k set are reranked directly, otherwise RC-CoT is generated to refine retrieval direction followed by full-corpus re-retrieval; (3) Training involves mining hard negatives to simulate realistic failures, joint optimization of direct and RC-CoT-augmented retrieval, and aligning the adviser with retrieval outcomes via supervised learning and retrieval-oriented reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MMEB-V2 and a diverse set of general multimodal retrieval benchmarks show that UniME-R1 consistently improves retrieval performance over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning retrieval reasoning on retrieval feedback (rather than query-only reasoning) is an effective paradigm for improving multimodal retrieval performance, as demonstrated by the UniME-R1 framework's consistent gains across benchmarks.

title: Bar-JEPA: Extracting Values from Bar Chart with Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture
summary: Bar charts are commonly used in data visualization, and while they are easily understood by humans, it is non-trivial to extract the underlying data computationally. For a machine-learning-based approach, training chart de-rendering models usually requires labeled, real-world data. Labeling data is a time consuming task, which is why annotated data is scarce. Models can learn more efficiently when provided with features of high semantic quality, which a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) is designed to learn in a self-supervised manner. We present a per-bar, numerical value recovery pipeline for bar charts, where a JEPA encoder is used to produce semantically rich latent features. The decoder model consuming these features is simple and quick to train and outputs the coordinates of ticks and bars, which can be used to recover bar values. The effectiveness of self-supervised finetuning and quality of the extracted features is evident when comparing our model to end-to-end supervised baselines. Code, datasets and checkpoints are available on \href{https://github.com/dralois/Bar-JEPA}{GitHub}.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a bar chart de-rendering pipeline that uses a JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture) encoder to produce semantically rich latent features, which are then fed into a simple, quickly-trained decoder to recover per-bar numerical values. The self-supervised approach outperforms end-to-end supervised baselines.
AI.motivation: Extracting underlying data from bar charts computationally is non-trivial. Machine-learning approaches require labeled real-world data, which is scarce due to the time-consuming nature of labeling. Models can learn more efficiently when provided with high-quality semantic features, which motivates using a self-supervised JEPA architecture.
AI.method: The pipeline uses a JEPA encoder trained in a self-supervised manner to produce semantically rich latent features from bar chart images. A simple decoder model consumes these features and outputs coordinates of ticks and bars, from which bar values are recovered.
AI.result: The model demonstrates effectiveness of self-supervised finetuning and the quality of extracted features, outperforming end-to-end supervised baselines. Code, datasets, and checkpoints are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Using a JEPA-based self-supervised encoder for bar chart de-rendering provides efficient learning and better performance compared to purely supervised approaches, helping address the scarcity of labeled chart data.

title: The Next Screenshot Knows: Gated Hindsight Distillation for Mobile GUI Agents
summary: GUI agents are commonly trained offline from successful interaction trajectories. Standard training decomposes each trajectory into prefix-action pairs: the agent predicts an action from the current screen and interaction history, while the subsequent observation is discarded. This removes the rationale of why an action is correct: the evidence often appears only on the subsequent screen. For example, to enable Soft Wrap, the agent should click Edit or View, but nothing reveals this until the menu opens. Without such evidence, standard imitation gives the model little chance of ever sampling and thus learning the correct reasoning. To address this issue, we propose Gated Hindsight Distillation (GHD), which uses the next screenshot as privileged information during training. A student predicts from the observable trajectory prefix, while a parameter-sharing teacher additionally observes the next screenshot and re-scores the student's on-policy responses. We apply distillation only when the student fails and the hindsight-conditioned teacher recovers the demonstrated action. GHD improves task success over GRPO on AndroidWorld and AndroidLab across two vision-language models. The code and checkpoints will be made available.

AI.tldr: Gated Hindsight Distillation (GHD) improves GUI agent training by using the next screenshot as privileged information during training, applying distillation only when the student fails but a hindsight-conditioned teacher recovers the correct action, outperforming GRPO on AndroidWorld and AndroidLab.
AI.motivation: Standard offline imitation training for GUI agents discards subsequent observations, removing the rationale for why an action is correct. Since evidence for correct actions often appears only on the next screen, standard imitation provides little opportunity for the model to learn correct reasoning.
AI.method: GHD trains a student from observable trajectory prefixes while a parameter-sharing teacher additionally observes the next screenshot and re-scores the student's on-policy responses. Distillation is applied only when the student fails and the teacher recovers the demonstrated action.
AI.result: GHD improves task success over GRPO on AndroidWorld and AndroidLab across two vision-language models.
AI.conclusion: Using next-screenshot hindsight as privileged information with gated distillation effectively improves GUI agent performance, and code/checkpoints will be released.

title: Domain-Grounded Candidate Selection for Agentic Image Editing: A Shadow Removal Case
summary: Commercial vision-language models are reshaping computer vision, with visual priors broad enough to rival task-specific systems. This raises a natural question: do they reduce the need for classic, physics-informed low-level vision? We study this through shadow removal, a problem shaped by scene geometry, illumination, materials, and occluders, where paired shadow and shadow-free data are hard to collect at scale. We find that a commercial generative editor, used directly, can produce clean shadow-free edits that preserve surface texture and local appearance. However, this comes with a new failure mode: the same editor can regenerate scene content, hallucinate objects, or misread a shadow as material or geometry, producing plausible but physically wrong edits. We address this with an agentic candidate-selection pipeline: the editor generates a guided probe, an evaluator screens for major failures, retries when needed, samples multiple candidates, filters them, and selects a final result balancing shadow removal against scene preservation. Grounding this process in shadow-formation physics makes it more reliable: prompting the generator and evaluator to treat shadows as illumination effects caused by light occlusion, not material or object structure, measurably improves quality and consistency. On the ShadowRemovalRefine benchmark, our physics-oriented pipeline achieves a CDD of 0.0075, reducing CDD by at least 47% over the strongest prior method. These results suggest that commercial vision-language models do not replace classic low-level vision priors; instead, such priors remain useful for constraining and steering physically underconstrained generation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether commercial vision-language models reduce the need for classic, physics-informed low-level vision, using shadow removal as a case study. It finds that while commercial generative editors can produce clean shadow-free edits, they suffer from hallucination and misreading of shadows as material/structure. The authors propose an agentic candidate-selection pipeline grounded in shadow-formation physics that achieves a CDD of 0.0075 on ShadowRemovalRefine, a 47% improvement over prior methods, demonstrating that physics-informed priors remain essential for constraining underconstrained generative models.
AI.motivation: To determine whether commercial vision-language models with broad visual priors can replace classic physics-informed low-level vision approaches, using shadow removal as a representative problem where paired data is difficult to collect at scale.
AI.method: An agentic candidate-selection pipeline: a commercial generative editor generates guided probes, an evaluator screens for major failures with retries, multiple candidates are sampled and filtered, and a final result is selected balancing shadow removal against scene preservation. The process is grounded in shadow-formation physics by prompting generator and evaluator to treat shadows as illumination effects from light occlusion, not material or object structure.
AI.result: On the ShadowRemovalRefine benchmark, the physics-oriented pipeline achieves a CDD of 0.0075, reducing CDD by at least 47% over the strongest prior method, with measurably improved quality and consistency.
AI.conclusion: Commercial vision-language models do not replace classic low-level vision priors; rather, such physics-informed priors remain valuable for constraining and steering physically underconstrained generation.

title: Dense-Cast: A lightweight ensemble of deep learning architectures for precipitation nowcasting
summary: Proper short-term forecasting of precipitation is crucial in disaster management and preparedness. Nonetheless, the variability and nonlinearity of precipitation make short-term forecasting challenging for meteorologists. Moreover, capturing temporal dependencies in spatiotemporal data is a challenge in precipitation nowcasting. In this article, we introduce a lightweight deep learning model for half-hourly precipitation nowcasting. This model has been designed by incorporating the DenseNet architecture, residual connections, and transformer encoders for effective precipitation nowcasting with reduced model parameters. The North-Eastern region of India has been selected as the area of interest for our study. The region receives the highest precipitation during the months of June-September due to the monsoon season. The proposed model takes the previous five time-steps of half-hourly precipitation as inputs and predicts the precipitation in the next two half-hours. The GPM IMERG precipitation dataset with a 30-minute cadence has been used in this study for training and testing the model. The proposed architecture achieves best MAE of 0.235 millimetres, RMSE of 0.735 millimetres, and KGE score of 0.816 at an interval of 30 minutes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a lightweight deep learning model for half-hourly precipitation nowcasting, combining DenseNet, residual connections, and transformer encoders. The model is tested on the North-Eastern region of India using GPM IMERG data, taking five previous half-hourly precipitation steps to predict the next two half-hours, achieving a best MAE of 0.235 mm, RMSE of 0.735 mm, and KGE of 0.816.
AI.motivation: Precipitation nowcasting is critical for disaster management but is challenging due to the variability and nonlinearity of precipitation, as well as difficulties in capturing temporal dependencies in spatiotemporal data.
AI.method: The proposed model is a lightweight deep learning architecture that integrates DenseNet, residual connections, and transformer encoders to reduce model parameters while effectively capturing spatiotemporal patterns. It uses five previous half-hourly precipitation time-steps as inputs to predict precipitation for the next two half-hours, trained and tested on the GPM IMERG precipitation dataset (30-minute cadence) for the North-Eastern region of India.
AI.result: The model achieves the best MAE of 0.235 mm, RMSE of 0.735 mm, and KGE score of 0.816 at a 30-minute interval.
AI.conclusion: The proposed lightweight architecture demonstrates effective and efficient precipitation nowcasting with strong error metrics, showing promise for practical operational use in rainfall forecasting applications.

title: Confidence matters: Leveraging Multi-view Geometric Priors for GS-based Reconstruction
summary: 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a widely-used tool for novel view synthesis, offering real-time rendering in a sparse representation. However, the method's reliance on structure-from-motion initialization and photometric optimization can lead to suboptimal geometric reconstruction, particularly for objects with high specularity. In this work, we investigate the integration of geometric priors, in the form of predicted normal and depth maps, into the 3DGS framework to improve the reconstruction quality. We analyze the effect of incorporating these priors into GS-based methods and our evaluation reveals that multi-view predictions, as they are done by the recent visual geometry grounded transformer (VGGT), outperform single-view alternatives. A major factor is the existence of a confidence map for the estimations, which comes as a by-product of multi-view models and which can significantly improve the effectiveness of priors by weighting each prediction appropriately. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show consistent improvement in reconstruction quality and significant gains in complex scenes including specular objects.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates integrating geometric priors (predicted normal and depth maps) into 3D Gaussian splatting to improve reconstruction quality, particularly for specular objects. It finds that multi-view predictions from VGGT with confidence maps outperform single-view alternatives, leading to consistent improvements on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: 3DGS relies on structure-from-motion initialization and photometric optimization, which leads to suboptimal geometric reconstruction for objects with high specularity. The paper aims to address this limitation by incorporating geometric priors.
AI.method: The authors integrate predicted normal and depth maps as geometric priors into the 3DGS framework. They compare single-view versus multi-view prediction approaches, using VGGT (visual geometry grounded transformer) for multi-view priors. Key to their method is the use of confidence maps derived from multi-view models to weight each prediction appropriately during optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show consistent improvement in reconstruction quality and significant gains on complex scenes with specular objects. Multi-view predictions with confidence-based weighting outperform single-view alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating multi-view geometric priors with confidence weighting into 3DGS significantly enhances reconstruction quality, especially for challenging specular scenes, demonstrating the value of principled prior integration.

title: Sample-Adaptive Latent Rewards for Uncertainty-Guided Diffusion Post-Training
summary: Latent reward models can supervise visual diffusion models without decoding intermediate states into pixel space. This makes alignment with human preferences more efficient. However, existing latent reward models output only scalar scores. They do not estimate the uncertainty of each prediction. The generator therefore cannot determine which feedback is reliable. This can drive optimization in the wrong direction and lead to reward hacking. We propose \textsc{SURE}, a unified latent-space framework for image and video diffusion models. It learns reward distributions and directly uses their reliability to guide dense post-training. First, we propose sample-adaptive latent reward model (\textsc{SURE-LRM}). It predicts a Gaussian utility for each noisy latent. Its mean predicts the reward score. Its variance reflect the uncertainty of prediction without human annotation. The learned distribution then guides post-training through uncertainty-guided reward feedback learning (\textsc{SURE-REFL}). This method provides uncertainty-guided dense feedback along the denoising trajectory. At selected transitions, \textsc{SURE-REFL} queries the frozen \textsc{SURE-LRM}. It converts detached variance into reliability weights for samples at the same transition. Each weighted reward is backpropagated only through its local transition. The entire process remains in latent space and requires neither pixel-space decoding nor the full denoising graph. Experiments show that \textsc{SURE-LRM} improves preference prediction over strong baselines. \textsc{SURE-REFL} achieves the sota performance among various metrics and further improves optimization stability. It also achieves the highest VBench quality, semantic, and total scores among the evaluated methods.

AI.tldr: SURE is a unified latent-space framework for image and video diffusion models that learns reward distributions with uncertainty estimates, using reliability weights to guide dense post-training without decoding into pixel space.
AI.motivation: Existing latent reward models only output scalar scores without uncertainty estimation, preventing generators from determining which feedback is reliable, which can drive optimization in wrong directions and lead to reward hacking.
AI.method: SURE consists of two components: (1) SURE-LRM, a sample-adaptive latent reward model that predicts a Gaussian utility for each noisy latent (mean as reward score, variance as uncertainty), and (2) SURE-REFL, an uncertainty-guided reward feedback learning method that provides dense feedback along the denoising trajectory using variance-derived reliability weights, with each weighted reward backpropagated only through its local transition in latent space.
AI.result: SURE-LRM improves preference prediction over strong baselines; SURE-REFL achieves state-of-the-art performance across various metrics, improves optimization stability, and attains the highest VBench quality, semantic, and total scores.
AI.conclusion: Modeling both reward scores and uncertainty in latent space enables more reliable and stable alignment post-training for diffusion models, avoiding pixel-space decoding and reward hacking.

title: Patient Pose Assessment Using a CT-Based Framework for Synthetic Data Generation
comment: Accepted for publication at the Journal of Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging (MELBA) https://melba-journal.org/2026:027
summary: An adequate diagnostic quality of radiographs is essential for reliable diagnoses and treatment planning. The patient's pose during radiography is one of the most important factors determining the diagnostic quality. Since patient positioning is difficult and not standardized, an automated AI-based approach using depth images to automatically assess the patient's pose before the radiograph has been taken would be helpful. Due to regulatory hurdles, however, it is difficult in practice to acquire the required depth images and corresponding radiographs. In this paper, we present a framework that can generate such training data synthetically from Computed Tomography scans. We further show that by pretraining on our generated synthetic dataset consisting of 3077 image pairs of upper ankle joints, the pose assessment of real upper ankle joints can be improved by up to 11 percentage points.

AI.tldr: A framework that generates synthetic depth image and radiograph pairs from CT scans to train an AI system for assessing patient pose before taking radiographs, improving pose assessment of real ankle joints by up to 11 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Patient positioning during radiography significantly affects diagnostic quality, but position assessment is difficult and non-standardized. Real paired depth images and radiographs are hard to acquire due to regulatory hurdles, so synthetic training data generation is proposed as an alternative.
AI.method: A synthetic data generation framework is built from Computed Tomography scans, producing paired depth images and corresponding radiographs. A dataset of 3077 image pairs of upper ankle joints was generated and used for pretraining a pose assessment model.
AI.result: Pretraining on the synthetic dataset improved pose assessment of real upper ankle joints by up to 11 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Synthetically generated paired depth image and radiograph data from CT scans is a viable approach to overcome regulatory data-acquisition hurdles and can meaningfully improve AI-based patient pose assessment in radiography.

title: Learning visual representations for compositional analysis of artworks and photographs
summary: Composition, the deliberate arrangement of visual elements, is central to how meaning, emotion, and aesthetic quality are conveyed in artwork, yet it remains among the least formalized dimensions of visual understanding. Prior work highlights a persistent gap in learning meaningful compositional representations, attributing it to semantic bias and suggesting that human-inspired approaches may be key. We compare two parallel paradigms for composition analysis: a human-inspired method grounded in perceptual grouping, and fine-tuned foundation models enabled by recent large-scale compositional datasets. The human-inspired approach uses object-centric models for region-level decomposition and a graph attention network to capture spatial relationships between elements. Both paradigms are evaluated on composition score/category prediction, compositional image retrieval, and visual saliency detection. With frozen encoders, the human-inspired method achieves competitive performance while remaining interpretable. When sufficient data enables fine-tuning, large self-supervised models outperform significantly, but at the cost of interpretability and cross-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two paradigms for visual composition analysis: a human-inspired approach based on perceptual grouping (object-centric models + graph attention networks) versus fine-tuned foundation models trained on large-scale compositional datasets. The human-inspired method is competitive and interpretable with frozen encoders, while fine-tuned self-supervised models outperform significantly but sacrifice interpretability and cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Composition is central to conveying meaning, emotion, and aesthetic quality in artwork, yet it remains among the least formalized dimensions of visual understanding. Prior work identifies a persistent gap in learning meaningful compositional representations due to semantic bias, suggesting that human-inspired approaches may be key to addressing this gap.
AI.method: Two parallel paradigms are compared: (1) a human-inspired method grounded in perceptual grouping, using object-centric models for region-level decomposition and a graph attention network to capture spatial relationships between elements; (2) fine-tuned foundation models enabled by recent large-scale compositional datasets.
AI.result: With frozen encoders, the human-inspired method achieves competitive performance while remaining interpretable. When sufficient data is available for fine-tuning, large self-supervised models significantly outperform the human-inspired approach, but at the cost of interpretability and cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: There is a clear trade-off between the two paradigms: human-inspired approaches offer interpretability and competitive performance in low-data settings, while fine-tuned foundation models provide superior performance when abundant data is available but lose interpretability and generalizability across domains.

title: BendTwin: Robust Dense-to-Sparse Physical Reconstruction with Bending-Aware Differentiable Spring-Mass Models
summary: Reconstructing objects with mechanical properties from video observations enables physically consistent dynamic prediction, benefiting robotics planning and interaction. Existing spring--mass based physical driven reconstruction approaches offer efficient and differentiable physical reconstruction, but they typically rely on axial springs alone. Such formulations oversimplify the underlying structural mechanics and can become mechanically under-constrained when the physical graph is coarsened, limiting their ability to preserve stable local deformation. We present BendTwin, a bending-aware differentiable spring--mass framework for video-based reconstruction and future prediction of deformable objects. BendTwin introduces bending stiffness and damping over local surface triplets, penalizing deviations from rest angles and regularizing higher-order deformation. These bending constraints improve mechanical stability while preserving the simplicity of spring--mass system. Experiments show that BendTwin consistently outperforms the axial-only PhysTwin baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate that the bending constraints maintain system stability across different downsampling ratios and consistently improve upon the original PhysTwin formulation. Overall, BendTwin provides an effective approach for constructing mechanically faithful digital twins from sparse-view RGB-D videos.

AI.tldr: BendTwin introduces bending stiffness and damping constraints over local surface triplets to a differentiable spring-mass framework, improving mechanical stability and reconstruction accuracy for deformable objects from RGB-D videos compared to axial-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing spring-mass based physical reconstruction approaches rely only on axial springs, which oversimplify structural mechanics and become mechanically under-constrained when the physical graph is coarsened, limiting their ability to preserve stable local deformation.
AI.method: BendTwin extends spring-mass systems by adding bending stiffness and damping over local surface triplets. These constraints penalize deviations from rest angles and regularize higher-order deformation, improving mechanical stability while maintaining the simplicity of spring-mass systems.
AI.result: BendTwin consistently outperforms the axial-only PhysTwin baseline. Ablation studies show the bending constraints maintain system stability across different downsampling ratios and consistently improve upon the original PhysTwin formulation.
AI.conclusion: BendTwin provides an effective approach for constructing mechanically faithful digital twins from sparse-view RGB-D videos, enabling physically consistent dynamic prediction for robotics planning and interaction.

title: Support Operation Factorization: Compositional Readout of Frozen Vision Encoders under Controlled Interventions
summary: Compositional analysis of frozen vision encoders should determine both what changed and where it changed. Standard factor probes score these axes separately, however, and can reward multiple operations that reuse the same predicted slot. We call this failure operation laundering. We introduce an injectively aligned leave-one-cell-out protocol over support x operation grids and SO-OPF, a readout that factors cell energy into support salience and a competitive operation posterior. This formulation separates two questions that aggregate scores conflate: whether the carrier composes held-out bindings when the grid is known, and whether that grid can be recovered from flat cell labels. With frozen DINOv3 features, known factorial assignment reaches 0.874 injective accuracy on Shapes3D-Extended and 0.799 on globally image-disjoint COCO; learning the assignment from flat labels reaches 0.769 and 0.762, respectively. Under matched-axis-aware supervision on Shapes3D, the factored carrier improves learned-assignment accuracy from 0.653 to 0.841 over a dense carrier and eliminates its laundering gap. SigLIP2 replicates the COCO separation. A rebuilt MuJoCo substrate exposes a boundary: learned-assignment accuracy is 0.569 with DINOv3 and 0.484 with SigLIP2, with substantial slot collapse. Thus factored readout and injective evaluation recover held-out bindings on two substrates while exposing, rather than hiding, a renderer-specific failure boundary; they do not establish universal recovery from flat labels.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an injectively aligned leave-one-cell-out protocol and SO-OPF readout to study compositional analysis of frozen vision encoders. It addresses "operation laundering"—a failure where factor probes reward multiple operations reusing the same predicted slot. The method factors cell energy into support salience and a competitive operation posterior, separating questions of composition given a known grid versus recovering the grid from flat labels. Results show strong performance on Shapes3D-Extended and COCO with DINOv3 and SigLIP2, but exposes a renderer-specific failure boundary on a rebuilt MuJoCo substrate, revealing that universal recovery from flat labels is not established.
AI.motivation: Standard factor probes for compositional analysis of frozen vision encoders score axes separately and can suffer from "operation laundering," where multiple operations reuse the same predicted slot, conflating whether the carrier composes held-out bindings versus whether the grid can be recovered from flat cell labels. The paper aims to separate these two distinct questions and provide a more principled evaluation protocol.
AI.method: Introduces an injectively aligned leave-one-cell-out protocol over support x operation grids, and SO-OPF (Support salience and Operation posterior Factorization), a readout that factors cell energy into support salience and a competitive operation posterior. This separates whether the carrier composes held-out bindings given a known grid from whether the grid can be recovered from flat cell labels.
AI.result: With frozen DINOv3 features, known factorial assignment achieves 0.874 injective accuracy on Shapes3D-Extended and 0.799 on globally image-disjoint COCO; learning assignment from flat labels reaches 0.769 and 0.762 respectively. On Shapes3D, the factored carrier improves learned-assignment accuracy from 0.653 to 0.841 over a dense carrier and eliminates its laundering gap. SigLIP2 replicates the COCO separation. A rebuilt MuJoCo substrate exposes a boundary: learned-assignment accuracy is 0.569 (DINOv3) and 0.484 (SigLIP2) with substantial slot collapse.
AI.conclusion: Factored readout and injective evaluation successfully recover held-out bindings on two substrates (Shapes3D and COCO) while exposing a renderer-specific failure boundary on MuJoCo rather than hiding it. The approach does not establish universal recovery from flat labels, highlighting the need for careful substrate selection and acknowledging limitations in generalization.

title: EvReflection: Event-Driven Micro-Dynamics for Reflection Removal
summary: Despite remarkable progress in reflection removal, current methods primarily exploit static image priors from a single frame and still suffer from severe residual artifacts due to the inherent ambiguity between the reflection and transmission layers. In this paper, we propose leveraging event signals to break this ambiguity. By employing event cameras to capture micro-dynamics, we reveal the differential motion between these two layers. We thereby present a novel event-driven reflection removal network, EvReflection, that utilizes these dynamic cues for layer separation. Specifically, we design a Micro-Dynamics Decoupler to disentangle layer-specific motions from event streams as priors, which then guide a Parallax-Attention Rectifier to cleanly remove artifacts from the RGB image. Furthermore, to address data scarcity, we develop a parallax-aware simulation pipeline and construct the EVR$^2$ benchmark dataset, the first real-world dataset for this task. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvReflection achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks, surpassing the best competing method by more than 1.6 dB and 1.2 dB in PSNR, respectively. The code, dataset, and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/JiaxiaoWang/EvReflection.

AI.tldr: EvReflection is a novel event-driven reflection removal network that leverages event camera signals to capture micro-dynamics and break the inherent ambiguity between reflection and transmission layers, outperforming existing methods by over 1.6 dB PSNR on synthetic and 1.2 dB on real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current reflection removal methods rely on static image priors from a single frame and suffer from residual artifacts due to the inherent ambiguity between reflection and transmission layers. The authors propose using event signals—which capture micro-dynamics and differential motion between layers—to break this ambiguity.
AI.method: The paper introduces EvReflection, an event-driven reflection removal network with two key components: (1) a Micro-Dynamics Decoupler that disentangles layer-specific motions from event streams as priors, and (2) a Parallax-Attention Rectifier that uses these priors to remove artifacts from the RGB image. Additionally, a parallax-aware simulation pipeline and the EVR² benchmark dataset (first real-world dataset for this task) are developed.
AI.result: EvReflection achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks, surpassing the best competing method by more than 1.6 dB and 1.2 dB in PSNR, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Event signals provide effective dynamic cues for reflection removal by revealing differential motion between layers, and the proposed method with its accompanying dataset establishes a new benchmark for this task.

title: HOPE: Hand-Object Pressure Estimation from Monocular Videos
summary: Estimating physical pressure from vision is essential for understanding contact-rich hand-object interaction. However, prior vision-based pressure estimation methods are largely limited to planar surfaces and single image input, making them difficult to apply to dynamic hand-object interaction with diverse objects. We instead formulate pressure estimation as a hand-centric video prediction problem with monocular video as input. This formulation predicts temporally evolving per-vertex normal pressure and contact directly on the hand mesh, yielding a unified output space independent of object shape and sensor layout. Building on this formulation, we propose \textbf{HOPE}, a framework with two key components. First, we lift tactile-glove pressure, planar-sensor pressure, and distance-based hand-object contact annotations into a shared hand vertex space, allowing bare-hand contact data to regularize pressure learning where metric labels are unavailable. Second, we introduce a vertex-anchored video transformer that treats each vertex as a persistent token, aggregates visual features and hand pose over time, and uses a contact-gated pressure head to enforce that pressure vanishes without contact. Experiments on OpenTouch, PressureVisionDB, and hand-object contact benchmarks validate HOPE across object-pressure, surface-pressure, and contact-supervised HOI settings. Despite using metric pressure supervision primarily from gloved-hand videos, HOPE generalizes to bare-hand egocentric and in-the-wild videos, producing joint contact and pressure predictions beyond the scope of contact-only or planar-pressure baselines.

AI.tldr: HOPE is a framework that formulates physical pressure estimation from monocular video as a hand-centric video prediction problem, predicting per-vertex normal pressure and contact directly on the hand mesh to unify output space independent of object shape and sensor layout.
AI.motivation: Prior vision-based pressure estimation methods are limited to planar surfaces and single image input, making them inapplicable to dynamic hand-object interaction with diverse objects.
AI.method: HOPE uses a hand-centric video prediction formulation with two key components: (1) lifting tactile-glove pressure, planar-sensor pressure, and distance-based hand-object contact annotations into a shared hand vertex space for regularization; (2) a vertex-anchored video transformer treating each vertex as a persistent token, aggregating visual features and hand pose over time, with a contact-gated pressure head.
AI.result: Experiments on OpenTouch, PressureVisionDB, and hand-object contact benchmarks validate HOPE across object-pressure, surface-pressure, and contact-supervised HOI settings. Despite metric pressure supervision primarily from gloved-hand videos, HOPE generalizes to bare-hand egocentric and in-the-wild videos.
